speechtext:
Hon. members are no doubt aware that on May 2 President Kennedy of the United States made an announcement drawing attention to his view that a long term solution on an international basis was required to deal with the problem arising from international trade in textiles.
A tripartite meeting at the official level has been arranged to be held in London next week on this subject. Canadian representatives will participate there in informal discussions with representatives of the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States to discuss these textile problems. It is expected that officials from the crown colony of Hong Kong will also participate in these discussions.
Canada has consistently supported previous attempts to find a comprehensive international solution to these problems; always, of course, without prejudice to Canada's freedom of action, under our trade agreements, to take measures to avoid injury to particular Canadian industries during the period when a broad international settlement is being negotiated.

subtopic: SHIP OPERATING AND SHIPBUILDING-STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
SHIP OPERATING AND SHIPBUILDING-STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are aware of the serious problems which during the last 15 years have faced the ship operating and shipbuilding industries in Canada in maintaining activity and employment in both fields.
This matter has been receiving the active consideration of the present administration since it took Office, and I wish to announce that a policy has been determined which will
be of major benefit both to our Canadian ship operators and to our Canadian shipyards. This policy is intended to make it possible for Canadian ship operators to obtain new vessels from Canadian shipyards at reasonable and competitive prices instead of being forced to have them built abroad because of the lower construction costs that prevail in other countries. It is also intended to make it possible for the Canadian fishing industry to obtain the necessary degree of assistance to encourage it to modernize its fleet by the construction of new vessels in Canadian shipyards on a basis which will still keep the costs to the Canadian fishing industry at a competitive level and halt the trend of construction of vessels for the Canadian fleet in other countries.
Finally, the policy is intended to deal with the situation which has emerged recently in the great lakes trade as a result of the arrangements which have made it possible for foreign vessels of commonwealth registry to participate in the domestic trade within this area.
To achieve the first objectives, namely assistance to our domestic operators and our fishing industry in obtaining new vessels from Canadian yards, parliament will be asked to provide, by way of departmental estimates, funds to assist in the construction of vessels for operation under Canadian registry whether in our domestic trades, in the fishing industry, or for use on the deep seas. A special capital subsidy of 35 per cent of approved costs of construction will be paid toward the construction in Canada of Canadian registry vessels, other than fishing vessels, whether for domestic or deep sea work, effective immediately. Moreover, to provide the maximum degree of incentive over approximately the next three years, this 35 per cent rate of assistance will be increased to 40 per cent for any work done between the present date and March 31, 1963. After that date the rate will be set at 35 per cent.
With regard to the fishing industry, a capital subsidy of 50 per cent of approved costs incurred from the date of this announcement will be paid toward the cost of the construction in Canada of steel fishing trawlers in any case where the new trawler will replace one old vessel which will be withdrawn from service. In addition, the present special assistance of up to 165 per gross ton payable toward the cost of construction in Canada

Government Policy in Shipbuilding of wooden fishing vessels over 45 feet in length will be increased to $250 per gross ton.
The foregoing assistance will be effective immediately, applicable to vessels now under construction and to vessels on which construction may be started hereafter. In the case of vessels now under construction, however, it is intended that the assistance will apply only to work which may actually be carried out from this day onward and not to construction work performed before this day.
The methods of determining approved costs for this purpose and other particulars relating to administration of this plan will be prescribed by regulations to be approved by the governor in council. These regulations will, of course, deal with the question of limiting the proportion of non-Canadian content to be included in costs for the purpose of the subsidies. These regulations have not yet been approved by the governor in council, but they will be tabled in the house as soon as they are in final approved form.
The government has also given considerable attention to another problem which relates to the great lakes area, and which has arisen since the royal commission on coasting trade made its report. Under the commonwealth merchant shipping agreement, a vessel of commonwealth registry may engage in the domestic coasting trade of Canada, and Canadian registered vessels enjoy reciprocal privileges in other countries. This agreement was made many years ago and long before the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. Prior to the construction of the seaway, deep sea vessels, other than those of very small size, did not have direct access to the great lakes, and in those waters which are basically inland waters the domestic coastal trade was more or less effectively reserved to Canadian registered vessels.
Within the last couple of years, in a number of cases old United States lake vessels which under the authority of the Canada Shipping Act would have been refused Canadian registry, have been purchased by certain operators who have applied for and obtained nonCanadian commonwealth registry with a view to putting those vessels in Canadian domestic service. In addition, other Canadian operators have moved in the direction of transfer of some of their existing great lakes vessels of Canadian registry to non-Canadian commonwealth registry.
Investigation has indicated that apparently under United Kingdom law applications for United Kingdom or colonial registry in cases of this sort have to be granted unless there is something technically wrong with the vessel itself, and there is no method under existing British law by which this condition of


affairs can be dealt with. Because the government believes in effect the domestic Canadian trade within the great lakes area was not in any sense contemplated as part of the reciprocal privileges when the commonwealth merchant shipping agreement originally came into force, and that this trade should be effectively reserved to Canadian registered vessels, accordingly the government has decided to initiate steps for modification of the commonwealth agreement to exclude this area.
For this purpose we will be approaching the other parties to this agreement to notify them of our decision to exclude from the provisions of this agreement the great lakes area, which will be defined as commencing at the outermost pilotage station in the St. Lawrence river in the vicinity of Les Escoumains. The effective date of this change, of course, can only be determined after notification to and consultation with the other commonwealth countries concerned and will, I expect, also involve amendment to the Canada Shipping Act.
This new policy will be of great benefit to Canadian ship operators and Canadian seamen as well as Canadian shipyards, and their employees and suppliers. It will help our domestic operators, whether these be inland, coastal or deep sea operators, and whether their craft be cargo vessels, passenger vessels, tankers or schooners on the St. Lawrence, or other powered craft of reasonable size.
It is virtually impossible to forecast accurately what this program will amount to in terms of expenditure and employment, since the initiative in making it successful must now rest with our ship operators themselves. However, at a very rough estimate I would expect this should cover more than 10,000 man years of additional employment in each year for the next few years in our shipyards, and probably an equal number in supporting and supplying industries, to say nothing of increased opportunities that may result for seafaring personnel.

Mr. Speaker, the shipbuilding industry will undoubtedly be interested in the statement which has just been made by the minister. It is certainly to be hoped the situation has not deteriorated to a position where it will take too long to rebuild it as a major Canadian industry.
In view of the outstanding record established by the Canadian shipbuilding industry both in peace and war it is perhaps surprising that this industry should have been allowed to deteriorate to the position it now occupies, in which so many of our shipyards are either closed or operating on short time. The statement of the minister covered three phases, all of importance. One of particular importance today is that relating to the fishing industry. Be that as it may, we express regret at the delay and the deterioration. We will make a careful study of the details when they are available. I think the western farmer is aware that never before have such efforts been made to move grain out of Canada as have been made in the last few months. I might mention in passing that as part of this program we have stepped up the capacity of the west coast ports to handle this traffic. In the month of April we shipped 19 million bushels out of there, and this month we expect to ship 20 million bushels. I am leaving this week end to see whether I cannot get another couple of million bushels.
From the great lakes, shipping is moving out at a pace away above last year. At the present time nearly a thousand cars of grain a day are moving into Fort William and Port Arthur, and between 300 and 400 cars daily are moving in the west coast ports.
In answer to the question asked by the hon. member, I should just like to say that on May 8 the official quotas in western Canada were as follows: 213 points were on a 2 bushel quota, 742 were on a 3 bushel quota, 394 were on a 4 bushel quota and 645 on a 5 bushel quota.
Now let me give the hon. gentleman the figures for three days later, May 11. On May

Mr. Chairman, last evening the hon. member for Gloucester presented some information which was contained in a publication of the British Columbia fisheries association in regard to fishing, as to the volume of fish caught by the Soviet union and the size of its fleet in two parts of the world.
I have now a reference to the effect that the Soviet fishing fleet has operated in the north Pacific. Canada, along with Japan and the United States, is a signatory to the international north Pacific salmon fisheries commission, a tripartite arrangement dealing with

conservation matters in an attempt to ensure that the salmon intermingling ground, which I hope is in the Japanese area and off the coast of Canada and the United States, is protected so that immature fish are not caught.
I believe about two years ago the Soviet union fishing fleet was seen in that particular area, although its primary concern at that time, as indicated by the Department of Fisheries, was directed toward the catching of groundfish rather than salmon. At that time members of the C.C.F. group expressed concern that the Soviet fishing fleet, not being a signatory to the north Pacific salmon fisheries commission, could very easily become involved in fishing for salmon in this intermingling area, and thus participate in the destruction or depletion of salmon stocks from Canadian grounds. Also raised at that time was the possibility that China may subsequently develop a fishing fleet which could also fish in these particular waters. The desire was expressed that the Soviet union initially, and China later on, should be approached in an attempt to have them become part of the north Pacific salmon fisheries commission as signatories, in an attempt to ensure that our salmon stocks are not depleted by fishing in the intermingling areas.
There are some problems involved here which hinge upon the attitude of the United States and Canada, which follows the United States in so far as the field of diplomacy is concerned. We all know that the United States has been adamant in its refusal to recognize, either diplomatically or in any other way, the people of the republic of China; and Canada, refusing to be independent in this regard, has followed suit. I think we can all see the difficulty that could arise if eventually China did develop a fishing fleet which would fish in the particular waters to which I refer, and we subsequently desired or felt that China should become a part of the north Pacific salmon fisheries commission. We can easily see that the silly attitude of the United States, followed by Canada, could pretty well prevent any sort of discussion which would lead to China and the Soviet union becoming a part of this particular commission.
In view of the fact that Russia does have a large fishing fleet and that just a few years ago, namely in 1956, she had only two or three ships out in the Atlantic and now has somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100, if I recall the figures quoted by the hon. member for Gloucester, it is most important that this matter should be taken into consideration. Two or three years ago there was a fleet of some 40 boats of the Soviet union in the Bering strait fishing area looking for ground-fish or halibut. If Russia and China should
Supply-Fisheries
develop a fishing industry, I think it is most important that they be approached with a view to becoming part of the north Pacific salmon fisheries commission in order to ensure that all classes of fish, both on the Soviet side and on the Canada-United States side, be protected and conserved to the fullest possible extent.
I wish to touch on a question in the discussion of which some people may say I am being rather critical of and unfair to certain parts of the country. I do not discuss this matter in the sense of being unfair but in order to deal with it in another way. It seems to me there is far more concentration of assistance-subsidies, grants and financial aid-to the fishing industry of the maritimes than there is to that of the west coast. For instance, I could refer to the Newfoundland bait service as a case in point. Activities under the Fisheries Prices Support Act have been primarily confined by practice to the Atlantic coast even though there is no geographical limitation to its operation. The bait freezing storage facilities also are confined pretty well to the Atlantic coast. The announcement made today by the Minister of Transport on a subject which has been discussed under fisheries estimates on a number of occasions, having to do with increased grants toward the cost of building certain types of fishing vessels such as draggers, long-liners and so on, relates to an activity that is confined to the Atlantic coast.
In introducing his estimates last night the minister said that courses for foremen in fish canneries would be conducted in the Atlantic provinces. After listening to and reading his remarks I take it that this is an activity in which the Department of Fisheries is going to participate in some way, although the minister's remarks were not clear as to just in what way; but again this is something which is confined to the Atlantic coast. The announcement of the Minister of Transport this morning of assistance to the shipbuilding industry in so far as fishing vessels are concerned indicated-from what I could grasp of it, and I stand to be corrected, because often when a long detailed statement of that nature is made one can get an incorrect impression- that the assistance in so far as fishing vessels are concerned will be confined to steel ships where those steel ships replace older or antiquated fishing vessels. And, as I mentioned earlier, the increase in the subsidy for long-liners and draggers will be confined primarily to the east coast also. I submit that this recent announcement will be of relatively little help or importance to the fishing industry on the west coast.

Supply-Fisheries
The point I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, and this is not by way of complaint or suggesting that the assistance should be decreased, is that this does point up the fact that perhaps the fishing industry on the east coast is in a generally worse economic condition than the fishing industry on the west coast. I do not think we can continue to attempt to deal with this problem merely from the point of view of the subsidies, grants and assistance that have been given under the various items of legislation I have mentioned, although certainly at the moment it appears that this is a necessary thing to do in order to ensure that the fishing industry on the east coast is maintained at the highest possible level.
If we say that we are going to approach this economic difficulty by means of subsidies, grants and other assistance, then the problem will never be overcome. I think there should be a far more intense examination of the conditions of the fishing industry on the east coast to see whether some other approach cannot be made to the problem so that the fishing industry in that part of the country will become more economic, more profitable and thus be enabled to function more on its own than on government grants, subsidies and aid.
We discussed this problem to some extent on an earlier occasion. One of the ways in which the problem can be met is by the development of co-operatives. Here I am getting into another field, of course, which involves provincial governments to some extent. I mention it only in passing. The basic point is that I do not think we can continue to look at the fishing industry, or any other industry for that matter, purely from the point of view of government grants, government aid, government subsidies, government hand-outs and the like. We must take a rather different and more concerted approach to this question to see whether the industry itself can become economic to the point where it does not have to rely upon assistance of this type.
Last year the herring industry on the west coast collapsed largely because of the glut of meal and oil in the world market, and I think primarily because of the impact of the increased Peruvian production. At that time it was advocated that perhaps we should take steps to regear the herring industry to one which produced herring for food rather than for fish meal and oil. It was also advocated that we seek as well to sell on the international market cured or fresh frozen or canned herring. China was mentioned as one of the countries to which sales of this commodity might be made.

Without mentioning their names or their political stripe I can remember some people saying that this was absolutely foolish because all China was interested in buying with her scarce dollars were guns and ammunition; they were not interested in herring or food of any sort. Yet just a few days ago, as well as on another prior occasion, the Minister of Agriculture was able to announce in the house and elsewhere the sale of Canadian grain to China because of the food shortage and other factors existing in that country. If there is immense overproduction of fish meal and oil on the world market, surely to heaven we should be seeking other ways and means to develop our herring industry, and I simply use that industry as one example because it was in extreme difficulties last year. Surely we should try to develop it to the point where we produce herring for food and attempt to expand the sale of that commodity to China, just as we have done in the case of grain. Regardless of the meeting which was held in Rome, I believe, not too long ago, if we continue to push herring production into meal and oil every other country does the same thing, we are not really solving the food problem or any other problem but are simply aggravating the situation. We are merely taking steps to lessen the difficulty as much as we can without really solving the problem.
I should like to deal with one specific point about which I have had a fair amount of correspondence over the last few years, and with which I am sure the department is familiar. It has to do with what are known as reef nets and their use in the Juan de Fuca strait area. Perhaps the best way to place this matter before the committee is to refer briefly to a letter I received some time ago from Chief Edwin Underwood, chief of the East Saanich Indian band, in which he sets out the problem involved because of the prohibition of the use of reef nets. The letter reads in part as follows:
The reel net was in use on this coast long before white men came here. Its use is an hereditary right and usage has never been surrendered by the Indians in any treaty or agreement. It should always be emphasized that reef nets are not fish traps.
Prior to 1916 the white man's fish traps as well as reef nets were in common use in the waters of Juan de Fuca strait and of the gulf of Georgia in both Canadian and United States territory. In 1916 the United States, by legislation, banned fish traps in the San Juan islands group but allowed reef nets to be used as reef nets were recognized as not being traps. Reef nets are in common use today on the United States side of the boundary by white men even more than by Indians.
At the same time the Canadian government banned fish traps in Canadian waters. Reef nets were apparently classed as traps, which they are not, and were also banned.

Without getting involved in the technical argument whether a reef net causes damage so far as conservation is concerned, or whether it is in fact the same as a fish trap within the meaning of our legislation, this is the point I want to get at and it is related to the rights of our Indian people. Reef nets were used prior to 1916 and were then banned by Canada as being the same as a fish trap. However, they are being used by United States fishermen in substantially the same area. If they are destructive so far as fishing interests are concerned, then in some way or other they should also be banned by the United States in that same area. But if they are not destructive, and it has been represented to me that they are not, the use of reef nets should be allowed in that particular area, especially by the native Indian people.
I understand that this matter has been discussed with the United States authorities, and perhaps the minister will indicate at a later stage what the department's position is with respect to reef nets and what arrangements, if any, they are seeking to work out with the United States with respect to their use in this area.
I should like to make another comment that also has to do with the Indians. For many years Indians on the west coast, in any event, have always had the right to fish for food for their own consumption at any time and at any place. I think the native Indian people have been misled in this regard, because I have seen letters dated as late as last year and signed by the Minister of Fisheries or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration which have stated specifically that this was a right of the Indian people, that it could not be touched and that was that.
When I visited the Queen Charlotte islands last fall I heard some complaints about this matter involving the placing of restrictions on fishing for pink salmon for food. The native people were complaining and were wondering what right the department had to interfere with their hereditary right to fish for food. I went to see the fisheries officer and discovered that the department has the right to do this sort of thing. I found that the native Indians do not have an hereditary right, and that in fact the right to fish is granted to them under sufferance.
The British Columbia fisheries regulations made under the Fisheries Act provide in regulation 32, which I do not intend to read, that an Indian can catch fish for food with the permission of the chief supervisor, and that this permission can be limited as to times, places, waters and types of fish, or such fishing can be prohibited entirely. I only raise this point in order to say that for
Supply-Fisheries
a long period of time the native people of British Columbia have been misled into thinking they had some inalienable and untouchable right which in fact they do not have, and I think in future some attempt should be made to point out this fact to the Indians.
There is one other activity in the field of fisheries in British Columbia about which there has been some controversy in recent months and years. This matter finally culminated at least partially in a report by Dr. Sol Sinclair of Manitoba. I should like to say generally that it seems to me that the engagement of someone outside the government service, especially outside the Department of Fisheries, to conduct a survey of this nature is somewhat of an affront to the officials of the department who, as I know them, are extremely able men and very much dedicated to their work. Not only with respect to the report of Dr. Sinclair but also other similar types of reports I have often wondered why it is necessary to by-pass and to some extent slight the officials of a department who are dedicated solely to the particular field in which they work. It seems to me that in the Department of Fisheries there are people who are astute and capable enough to have made such a study, and to have arrived at recommendations or suggestions somewhat similar to those of Dr. Sinclair.
While I am on the subject of Dr. Sinclair's report on licence limitation, I should like to ask the minister to give the committee when he replies on the first item, or at a subsequent stage of his estimates, an indication of the attitude of the government with respect to the various far-reaching and important recommendations made by Dr. Sinclair. I know that the report has been in the minister's hands for only a short period of time, but I think he should be able to bring us up to date as to what the government intends to do with respect to Dr. Sinclair's recommendations. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the same course of action with regard to this report is not taken as was taken with regard to the report of the royal commission on food prices, which recommended a federal fish marketing act. The minister said a few days ago that this recommendation would be bypassed for a period of time.
I should also like the minister to give an explanation to the committee concerning the artificial spawning grounds. I believe two or three years ago there were some experiments in this field which were primarily directed toward the pink salmon, on the understanding that these experiments would be extended to other species found on the coast. I wonder if the minister could bring us up to date on the progress being made in connection with artificial spawning grounds for all species.

Supply-Fisheries
In addition, some studies were being made into the efficacy of aureomycin used as a fish preservative. I should appreciate some comments from the minister as to what has been discovered in this particular field, whether or not aureomycin has been found to be an efficacious fish preservative, keeping in mind the physiological effects of aureomycin on the consumer. While it may well be that aureomycin or some other antibiotic will be found to be a good preservative of fish, we must take into account the effect it is going to have on the consumer.
In find I am within a minute or two of my 30 minute allotment, Mr. Chairman, so perhaps I could conclude at this point. I am quite sure there will be ample opportunity during the consideration of these estimates for other specific matters to be discussed.

Since I am following the hon. member for Skeena, I might say that between us we represent the major part of the coastline of British Columbia. We are, consequently, aware of most of the problems connected with the fisheries. While we do not always agree on the solutions to these problems, we are both very much concerned with them and are endeavouring to do our best to find solutions.
The Comox-Alberni constituency is probably one of the major fish producing areas of Canada. The major portion of the salmon and shellfish catches is made along the shores of Comox-Alberni. One of the major problems of the fisheries in Comox-Alberni, which probably does not exist to the same extent in the riding to the north, is the ever increasing pressure of sports fishing on the salmon population and its effect on conservation.
Some people are misled about this sports fishing catch. They seem to think something is being taken away from the commercial fishermen and is, therefore, a loss to the economy. This is not the case by any means. About 40 per cent of the total salt water sports catch is made in the waters off Comox-Alberni. Sports fishing is responsible for a tremendous revenue in connection with the tourist business. So when it comes to the question of the greatest return from the trolled salmon catch in this area, the weighted evidence is in favour of the sport catch. It is safe to say that an average of $20 is expended for gear, boats, boat rentals, etc., for every fish caught by a local sportsman. My seatmate, the hon. member for New Westminster, says I am much too conservative. He says that every time he catches a fish it costs him $250. I do not know what he spends all that money on.

It is safe, however, to say that the figure for expenditures by foreign tourists for transportation, accommodation, gear purchases, boat rentals and so on would be in the neighbourhood of $100 per fish. Sports fishing, therefore, is responsible for a large part of the income derived from tourists on Vancouver island. It is for this reason it is so important that everything possible be done to preserve and enlarge the runs of spring salmon and cohoe, particularly in the sports fishing areas.
In this connection, the department is to be congratulated upon the construction of its Robertson creek controlled spawning ground, which has proven eminently successful, and for embarking upon the construction of the project on the Big Qualicum river. These projects will not only assist materially in maintaining salmon runs, but it is hoped they will substantially increase them. I would ask the minister to have his officials make a careful appraisal of the salmon runs in the Campbell River area with a view to the development of controlled spawning projects in that area, as well as the general improvement of natural spawning grounds. The Campbell River area is famous the world over as a sports fishing area, and has been for over half a century. The revenue from tourists who come to Campbell River is tremendous. Local organizations such as the chamber of commerce and a new one recently formed called Salmon Unlimited, are rightfully concerned over what appears to them to be a depletion in the runs in that area.
Along the east coast of the island we have another river which has presented a problem for a number of years. I refer to the Punt-ledge river. I have raised this question in the house before. The present condition of this river, from a fish conservation point of view, is the result of a power development by the British Columbia power commission in 1955 and 1956. The waters off the mouth of the Puntledge and Courtenay rivers have always been famous sports fishing areas. This is one of the areas in which the famous tyee or king salmon is found. In 1957 the spring salmon run was virtually destroyed on its way to the spawning grounds. I expect the effects of this will be noticeable this year, and again there will be a lack of tyees in 1962. The department has made an effort to ensure an adequate spawn and successful seaward escapement of smolts, but this has been an expensive and, I think, a short term answer. The fisheries research branch and its officers have made an exhaustive survey and developed a plan they hope will solve the problem. I understand that several years ago the department requested the power commission to make certain installations for fish

protection. Admittedly they are expensive; I understand the cost is in the neighbourhood of $750,000, but the expenditure is minor when related to the tourist revenue of the Comox-Courtenay area.
I know it is the financial responsibility of the power commission to make the proposed installations, but I think it is also the responsibility of the federal Department of Fisheries to see that immediate action is taken. Over a year ago the B.C. power commission referred the matter to the B.C. energy board, which as yet has not rendered a decision. What authority that body has to decide on a federal matter-and this is purely a federal matter-is beyond my comprehension. I think it is time the minister insisted that the power commission get on with the job of making the necessary improvements to this river in order that the salmon runs may be protected.
I should like to make a few comments on what is now the well known, at least in British Columbia, Sinclair report. This report was prepared by Dr. Sol Sinclair at the request of the department, and a great deal [DOT]of work was involved in it. I understand that Dr. Sinclair is rated as one of the foremost economists in agriculture. In his report, as I read it, he does not give proper consideration to economics in his discussion of sport salmon fishing. As I have previously pointed *out, a salmon caught by a tourist leaves far more money in a community than one caught by a commercial fisherman. This is particularly so in the case of foreign visitors to British Columbia. Let us not delude ourselves; that is the primary reason for most of the visitors coming to this area. If our tourist industry is to survive we must continue to encourage United States visitors. They have plenty of scenery in their own country, but the one thing that will bring them to Vancouver island is the opportunity to catch a fish, or more fish than they can catch in their own waters.
Dr. Sinclair made a recommendation concerning the licensing of sports fishermen for purposes of control and conservation. I cannot support licensing in the sense of a licence which has a fee attached to it. However, if licensing is necessary for conservation purposes, licences should be issued in a manner similar to our forest service camp fire permits, where no fee is attached.
Dr. Sinclair has built up a very strong case for the limitation of the number of commercial fishing licences. However, I believe that some of the statistical material he used does not in fact give a true picture of the situation. I am always a little suspicious of statistics, because I have helped to fill out many statistical reports in my life time, and
Supply-Fisheries
I must admit that I was not always too careful about giving accurate information.
As an example of what I have said, let us take the figures given at the gross and net income of a troll fisherman. These are found on page 246 of Dr. Sinclair's report. It appears obvious that anyone who has taken out a commercial licence-I believe they cost $1 at present-and sold a fish is included in the statistics used in arriving at those figures, because they show a very, very low income for the average commercial troller. Approximately 54 per cent of them are shown as selling less than $500 worth of salmon in a season.
Everyone familiar with the fishing industry of British Columbia knows that commercial licences are obtained for a number of reasons. A large number are obtained by people who are classed as moonlighters. We have had a number of labour disputes in my province in the last few years, and I know that when there is a strike in the woods, the next day you will find most of the loggers out having a good time fishing. They have taken out commercial licences and are classed as commercial fishermen.
Another group are the white collar workers and others who are fond of fishing and who hope to recoup some of the cost of their recreation by the sale of their catch. Then there are pleasure boat owners who use their fishing licences as a basis for claiming sales tax exemption on parts and material used in the maintenance of their boats as well as in the purchase of gear. Another group are the wives and dependents of fishermen, who use this as a means of avoiding income tax. Therefore to arrive at a conclusion from statistics showing the average sale of the commercial troller is hardly well founded. The categories I have mentioned represent perhaps one third of the licensed troll fishermen, and I am sure they account for the pitifully low earning figure Dr. Sinclair has arrived at in his calculations.
The recommendation he made for an increase in the cost of commercial licences and for a minimum $40 boat licensing fee may have some merit, provided special consideration is given to the native Indian fisherman. The native Indian fisherman is hardly in a position to afford a high fee and if this recommendation is ever implemented I do not think native Indian fishermen should be subjected to this kind of licence fee.
However, Dr. Sinclair's conclusion that the elimination of the itinerant fisherman will necessarily result in an increased catch by those who fish as a full-time occupation is not sound, because a very large proportion of this latter group fish in areas in which sportsmen and itinerant fishermen do not

Supply-Fisheries
fish. For instance, I believe the major part of the troll catch of salmon is caught off the west coast of Vancouver island in an area where there is very, very occasional sports fishing. I further believe that the suggestion of licence limitation by direct government control should be dismissed as impracticable under any government other than a totalitarian one.

Mr. Chairman, each year when the Minister of Fisheries brings his estimates before the committee it is a time of great interest to us who are from a province which for many, many years-ever since its discovery, in fact-depended either wholly or in part upon the fisheries. Last night I listened with great interest to the minister as he reported to the committee. I also listened with great interest to the observations of the hon. member for Gloucester, and I should like to associate myself with them.
I should like to begin by saying that any suggestions which I make involving the spending of money by the government are to be regarded as asking the government to invest rather than to give. As far as possible, the suggestions I shall make lie along the lines of investment. I do not think it is either right or wise to ask for government support simply for the sake of getting money to spend. I do believe, however, that the government should look with favour upon the spending of money which is an investment and which will result in the government getting back its bread, so to speak, with butter on it.
With respect to the encouragement of the fisheries on the Atlantic coast-or perhaps I had better address myself specifically to the fisheries in Labrador and Newfoundland-I am satisfied that the expenditure of money in certain directions would constitute an investment which would be profitable not only to the fishermen themselves, particularly on the Atlantic seaboard, but to the Canadian economy as a whole. I think there has been a tendency, perhaps an understandable one, to overlook the value of ancient industries. Fishing is one industry which we have had with us for as long as there has been a Canada. As time went by and Canada developed from the first colony of Great Britain into the great nation she is today, as central Canada became industrialized and prosperous and as western Canada began to supply food of another kind for world consumption, decreasing attention was given to what was a great industry and what still is a basic industry. It was the first industry which produced food in the new world and, in my opinion, it could become an even greater industry than it has been in the past. The population of Newfoundland is increasing, and

the population of Canada is increasing, so it is important that the old industries be revitalized and extended just as the new industries should be encouraged and extended.
With this in mind I should like to make certain suggestions applicable to the fishermen and the fishing industry in my riding; suggestions which will, I hope, receive the attention of the minister and, beyond that, sympathetic scrutiny leading eventually to the investment of funds in this industry to the greater profit of my fishermen and of the Canadian people.
Briefly, the fishing industry can be broken up into three sections, production, processing and marketing. With respect to marketing, most of the problems under this heading properly concern the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have already spoken on that subject. However, there are some aspects, particularly in connection with the processing of fish, which are the business of the Department of Fisheries, and I shall have something to say about that later.
The production of fish begins, of course, with the fishermen and depends to a large extent on whether the fishermen have the necessary gear, the necessary facilities and the necessary supplies. There are some exceptions to this rule. Last year, for instance, fish did not appear at all in certain areas but, generally speaking, the equipment which a fisherman possesses has a great deal to do with whether or not he himself can make a living. This factor is, of course, all-important. The fisherman must make a living at his vocation; if he cannot, he is not able to remain in it without receiving aid which, perhaps, is not justified.
Making aid available to help the fisherman produce is a different thing entirely, and I think government assistance should begin right there with the fisherman; assistance designed to help him produce more. Much has been done in the past along these lines, but I do think there have been some basic aspects of this question which have been overlooked.
To begin with, I might mention the matter of the fisherman's ability to purchase his equipment and supplies. It happens from time to time that a fisherman finds that his gear is worn out, his engine is old, and his boat needs to be replaced. He discovers he has not made enough money or has not been able to set aside sufficient funds over the years to make the necessary replacements. If he is to replace his boat at all he has therefore to borrow the money, to obtain credit somewhere. This is not always easy, particularly in Labrador where it is a fact that better boats and equipment would definitely mean higher production per man. So we come to the

matter of small loans for fishermen, and despite what has been done so far there is not in existence, in my opinion, any scheme by which fishermen can borrow relatively small amounts of money for the purchase of boats, engines and equipment.
In the first place, in the remote settlements and in the smaller outports where fishing is carried on as a main industry today there are not the banking facilities available, and it is difficult for fishermen to take advantage of any loan scheme which may now exist. I ask the minister to consider seriously the possibility of having a loan scheme worked out whereby fishermen who need small loans so they may improve their property and increase their production may be assisted by some scheme which would make this money more easily available. In this respect I do not believe the fisherman has the same advantage the farmer enjoys, and I maintain that the Canadian fisherman must be placed on a par with the Canadian farmer. Both are producers. Both are necessary to our economy. The fisherman of the Atlantic coast should be given an opportunity to find the necessary money in order to equip themselves to continue in business.
In his announcement earlier today concerning assistance to shipbuilding, we heard the Minister of Transport say that the present special assistance of up to $165 per gross ton in connection with the construction in Canada of fishing vessels over 45 feet in length would be increased to $250 per gross ton. While that is $50 short of what my friend the hon. member for Gloucester requested last evening, we must be pleased that it is a step in the right direction, toward implementing a policy of assistance in the building of ships. I would point out that this assistance is primarily directed to the shipbuilding industry. I say that without in any way wishing to detract from what has been said in this regard this morning. This proposed measure will provide support and assistance to the Canadian shipbuilding industry by helping fishermen buy boats in Canada, although they could perhaps buy cheaper ones outside Canada. However, I repeat that this is a step in the right direction, but suggest that more than this is needed.
This assistance applies to vessels over 45 feet in length. Many of the boats operating along the coast of my riding are much smaller than that. These boats operate in the inshore fishing industry comparatively close to shore. I understand that for economic reasons it is not practical to operate a larger boat in this field. Many fishermen will not be able to take advantage of this assistance because the majority, at least in my area, use boats smaller than the 45-foot minimum, and the
Supply-Fisheries
introduction of the use of larger boats for this type of work is not feasible.
Just as the invention of traps increased fishery production during at least part of the year, the introduction of long liners in the appropriate field will do the same, but the inshore fishermen must still use small boats. To help the small operator, who must use a small boat to effectively do his work, assistance must be given toward the building of small boats as well as larger ones. The field in which these small boats operate represents a basic part of the fisheries industry, and I should ask the minister to sympathetically consider that situation.
The subject of small marine works should possibly be discussed when we are considering in detail the estimates of the Minister of Public Works. However, I think it is proper that I mention at this time that small marine works are nearly always used in the small fishing communities in the carrying out of their trade. Small wharves for fishing boats represent an essential part of the fishing trade in small communities, and there exists a need for an enlargement of the program of building these works. On this subject I should state that the community stage program, by and large, was a success. I was pleased to hear the minister say that it is intended that this program be continued, but sorry to hear that it is going to be continued on a diminished scale.
I should like to comment briefly in regard to this program. The building of community stages has provided very essential facilities for fishermen in a number of communities in Newfoundland. In addition to providing the property from which fishermen can fish this has had the tendency to bring fishermen together in groups and encouraging co-operative action on the part of the fishermen. Provision of these stages has also been of great economic benefit, because it is not easy any more for fishermen to acquire the necessary materials to build the old type fishing stages. The introduction of the new type community stage has provided the essential property for the use of fishermen.
Actually I should like to have heard that the program of building community stages was going to be continued at its former rate by the federal government, and I am sorry that this program has stopped following the provision of 20 such stages. I feel the government should have instituted a program to build perhaps 10 stages per year, carried on until all those areas which require them had been provided with the necessary stages. I feel that stages costing over $25,000 should be considered the responsibility of the federal government, and I suggest this would in no way have interfered with the ability of

the federal and provincial governments to make joint arrangements for the building of stages.
I repeat that it is my earnest opinion that the program of building community stages, which the federal government has now completed with the building of the twentieth stage, should be continued. It is a pity that the many communities which so badly need these stages will temporarily have to do without them, and I seriously ask the minister to give further consideration to the continuance of this program in Newfoundland and Labrador in addition to the program he informed us last night had been worked out with the provincial governments.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some further remarks a little later, regarding the type of stage needed, but intend to refer now to the other basic requirement of fishermen. Fishermen must have bait.
