Mr. Chairman, when the committee took recess at one o'clock I was endeavouring to establish the need for help to the fishermen so they could be independent and so that their production would increase. As a matter of fact, my arguments were based on the need for fishermen to be able to make a living. I pointed out that if the fisherman could not make a living at his job he could not continue at it without getting the kind of assistance which perhaps was not justified, or words to that effect. I hasten to say that by that I did not mean that fishermen should not get social assistance where needed, but I did mean that they should get the kind of aid that would make them independent in their vocation so that they would be able to maintain themselves, and not need other help.
In outlining some of the things which I thought could be done I was discussing, I think, when the committee rose, the question of bait supplies. Each year a shortage of bait cuts down the earning power of the fishermen. It is a perennial problem and I am very glad to see that this matter of bait supplies is one to which the federal Department of Fisheries has been giving attention. The bait holding units which are being installed have had a good effect. I request, of course, that this program be continued and that more of those bait holding units be

supplied to the fishing settlements in Newfoundland and in particular the fishing settlements in my riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. I request that the minister continue to give earnest attention to the matter of bait supplies for fishermen.
Again I request that the matter of manufacturing artificial bait be given very active consideration. I will not go into details, as I have done so already in this house, save to say that if the same attention were given to developing artificial bait for codfish as has been given to the development of artificial bait for sport fishermen the problem would have been solved long ago.
With respect to salt supplies, nearly every year there is a shortage of salt in various areas. This is perhaps not so much the responsibility of the federal government as it is of the fish trade itself and the fish merchants themselves. Although in these remarks I am trying to point out what I think are the duties of the federal government, I would not want to leave the impression that I think the whole fishery business should be run by the federal government. I think of the industry itself, the commercial interests which exploit the fisheries. They have their duties also. I would ask the federal government to keep on eye on the matter of salt supplies as well as bait supplies and give what assistance they can.
With respect to the processing of fish, there seems to be an overproduction, if anything, or perhaps an out of balance production of heavy salted fish, and this fish is sold in a highly competitive market. At the same time a good market exists for light salted fish. I do not believe we are producing enough light salted fish to fill the requirements of this market. In the old days light salted fish was produced chiefly by hand labour. Of course, it is unthinkable to consider going back to the old ways of making fish when those who made the fish were paid very little for their work. Today, heavy salted fish is chiefly made in mechanical driers. My plea is for a drier which will produce light salted fish.
My understanding is that one of the reasons why light salted fish cannot be made artificially is that it can be kept only a comparatively short time before going bad. In other words, when a fisherman light salts his fish he has to get rid of it fairly quickly in order for it to be made or else it will spoil. That being so, it would seem to indicate that cool rooms built in connection with community stages might be the answer. A community stage would be a unit consisting of a cool room, a bait holding unit and, of course, the stage itself. I said before lunch that I wanted to come back to the matter of community stages and one of the

points I had in mind was that a community stage program with the necessary cool rooms and bait holding units is necessary if we are to exploit the light salted fish business properly. It seems to be evident that there is a market for light salted fish, a market that is larger and more readily available than are the markets for heavy salted fish.
With respect to community stages on the Labrador, in addition to those built for Labrador residents I should also like to see the experiment tried of a community stage complete with a bunkhouse and dining facilities so that crews from elsewhere could spend the summer fishing on the coast and then sell to collectors, the fish caught and stored in the stage. That could very well be one way in which the Labrador fishery could be revitalized. Certainly Labrador offers some of the most prolific fishing grounds in Canada and Canada's are the best in the world.
There is no need for me to point out again how other nations are profiting by using the waters off Canada's coast. The Labrador floater fishery, which almost disappeared several years ago, shows sign of reviving and I believe that a new Labrador fishery tailored to meet present-day requirements is a distinct possibility. It is something that the minister could very well look into and I believe it would be rewarding to the fishermen as well as being of great benefit to the Canadian economy.
I should like to express appreciation for the work the minister's department is doing in research and again make a request for further study of the artificial drying of light salted fish. I believe this is absolutely essential. If we do not keep these markets then the markets will disappear. If the product to which they have been accustomed in the past is kept away from them long enough, the demand for it will completely cease to exist. It would be really tragic if we were to lose these historic markets, and if we do not develop the kind of product which the market wants somebody else is going to do it and we may well lose the market forever.
The question of what to do with respect to the fisheries is, I think, fairly easily answered. There have been commissions from time immemorial that have looked into the matter of what is wrong with the fisheries and some of these commissions have produced very valuable information. The last one was the Walsh commission in 1952, I believe, and as a result of that commission action was forthcoming. I ask the minister to keep an eye on the possibilities for development based on the knowledge he already has and so that he may acquire further knowledge I invite him and his officials to visit Labrador and
Supply-Fisheries
northern Newfoundland personally as soon as possible. When he has assessed what is needed, when he has acquired the necessary information, which is already at his disposal, all I ask him to do is to put into effect the policies that are needed. Some of these policies are simple. Some of them are very basic. They have to do with enabling the fishermen to produce more fish in order to make more money. Some of these policies, like the development or continuation of research, are more involved, but none of the problems is insurmountable. All are problems that can be met, and certainly with a knowledge of what is needed the will to do must be forthcoming.
I should also like to mention the presence of a Russian icebreaker at the seal fishery this year. This is a sign of the times, a sign of the increasing competition with which we are going to be faced in every phase of the fishing industry. It probably would not be a bad idea for us to consider at the appropriate time the advisability of having icebreakers available for the assistance of Canadian sealing ships.
I believe that the government of Newfoundland is experimenting at present with a new type of trawler. While I understand it is hoped that the boat will be self-sustaining, I might suggest to the minister in passing that as the knowledge gained will be available to all of Canada the federal government might consider sharing the loss with the province in the event there is a loss.
Finally, may I again emphasize the necessity of the investment of comparatively small sums of money so that the fishery can be more profitable for all concerned, so that fishermen will be more independent, so that fish products will bring a greater profit to Canada and so that the industry will grow faster than it has been and in proportion to our population and our economic needs to the greater profit of the fishermen of Canada and the people of Canada generally.

Mr. Chairman, as the representative from Queens-Lunenburg, one of the oldest and most famous fishing constituencies in Nova Scotia, it is with pleasure that I rise to participate in the debate on the fisheries estimates. My first words will be to commend the minister for the conscientious manner in which he is administering the affairs of his department. The fish and shellfish resources that abound off the coasts of Canada make a great material contribution to our national economy and to the food supplies of this nation and other countries, and they merit continual attention not only from the government but from private agencies as well.

Supply-Fisheries
The fishing industry is soundly based upon a living, constantly renewing source of national wealth which, with proper management and careful planning, can be maintained at its present level and greatly enlarged. However, if this resource is neglected or overexploited the reverse is true, and this presents Canadian fishermen with a constant problem. Supervision of this great resource is a governmental responsibility but in order to achieve the maximum results co-operation is required from all those engaged in the fishing industry, the fishermen, fishing companies, processors, dealers and the public at large.
The Department of Fisheries has made great forward strides under the present minister, with special emphasis on the fisheries research board. This progressive arm of the fisheries department has been conducting studies on oceanography and the fisheries, and I believe the information gained will be invaluable to Canada's fishermen.
We too easily forget that the earth's surface is only one quarter land and that almost three quarters is covered by water. Of the land quarter only about one half is habitable, and much less than that is cultivatable. On the habitable portion of the land, there now live about three billion people, approximately one billion more than lived here 50 years ago. Experts estimate at present rates of population growth there will be four billion in 15 years, and six billion or twice the present world population in a span of only 40 years. These numerous new people will need both space and food. If the world is to be called upon to provide additional food for another billion people in 15 years, a more readily available source than bringing new land under cultivation will almost certainly have to be found. The only large and as yet not fully explored source of food is the ocean. Recent and continuing heavy capital investment in large modern highly mechanized fishing fleets and in research and oceanographic vessels by the United Kingdom, the United States, Russia, France, Japan and indeed by most of the countries of the world seems to indicate that the race for animal protein is already under way.
We are carrying out similar studies in Canada. In fact, the Canadian committee on oceanography was reorganized in December 1959. From studies already made it would appear the great future developments in marine fisheries lie in three directions. One is to develop fish culture or fish farming. The second is to make fuller use and to take some of the guesswork out of the bank and ground-fish industry with which we are already familiar, and the third is to separate the productive from the non-productive areas on the 
many fishing banks that exist on our continental shelf. With the help of other governmental departments, these broader aspects of oceanography are no longer frightening and positive programs can be laid down and in due course carried out.
One of the prominent examples of fish farming is the experimental work carried out by the department with several imported varieties of oysters, seeking a breed which could survive in Nova Scotia waters. Efforts to plant Prince Edward Island oysters in the Atlantic coast regions of Nova Scotia have not been too successful. I understand from reports that there was extremely heavy mortality in the St. Margaret bay area, though some oysters did grow fairly well at coves near Chester. The reason these tests were not entirely successful could well be due to the fact water temperatures on the Atlantic coast are much colder than in the sheltered Northumberland strait area, and I suggest the department continue with these tests by bringing in oysters that are accustomed to colder waters.
Without question, any expenditure by the fisheries department in an effort to re-establish the oyster fishery depleted by the epidemic oyster disease some years ago can be readily justified because of the great economic benefits to the province, and the nation as a whole. The fact that this type of fishery is within three miles of our coast and will be of direct value to Canadian fishermen should be considered. I often wonder if Canadian fishermen realize the tremendous potential in the oyster fishery.
In 1960 for example we exported to the United Kingdom, British Guiana, St. Pierre and the United States a total of 19,200 pounds valued at $5,443. However, during the same period we imported from Hong Kong, Japan and the United States a total of 71,743 gallons of oysters weighing approximately 10 pounds per gallon, valued at $503,770. In other words, there is a market for over half a million dollars worth of oysters right here in Canada and these shellfish lend themselves well to farming. Plans are available whereby fishermen living along the coast could build cement holding ponds and by pumping in sea water under controlled temperatures, and using proper feeding plans, a suitable oyster harvest could be secured. Oyster seed farming is biologically possible if oyster seed of disease resistant strain is used, as proved on Conway narrows flats in Prince Edward Island, the department's experimental area.
This calls for some forethought and planning, but this could be developed for the benefit of our inshore fishermen and could provide much needed revenue and employment in some of our Atlantic coast regions. The

market potential is not only great in Canada, but this program of oyster farming, if developed, could provide us with more oysters for export as the market for this succulent seafood is almost unlimited and this would improve our imbalance in trade. I believe the Bras d'Or lakes of Cape Breton, for example, with an entrance and exit to the sea, and where the water is warm enough to encourage excellent growth in a sheltered area, could be turned into one gigantic oyster farm bringing much needed income to the citizens of that area.
While commending the minister and the scientists of the research board for their efforts to replenish the oyster stocks in Nova Scotia, I would also urge they give equal attention to developing and restocking our clam beds along the Atlantic coast and our scallop beds in the bay of Fundy. During the past few years it has been found necessary to curtail clam digging in many areas of the Atlantic provinces because of the toxic effect this tasty seafood had on the consuming public, due to water pollution. As a result, many of our clam canning factories have been forced to close or seriously curtail their production, resulting in a further loss of income to our inshore fishermen. We see Japanese canned clams in constantly increasing quantities in the food stores throughout Canada, and to see this shellfish packed in a distant country offered for sale in the Atlantic provinces is the height of irony.
The fact that Japan, with its teeming millions in need of food, can export clams to Canada is indicative that we as a nation have been negligent in the care of our shellfish resources. Their success is not due to discoveries of which we are unaware, but due to their insistence in keeping up to date methods of development, production, inspection and conservation. What is the problem affecting our clam industry? In certain areas water pollution has been quite heavy, and as most people know shellfish will pick up and concentrate germs. However, it is equally true that contaminated shellfish will readily cleanse themselves in clean water. This is cheap and handy enough, but to ensure and certify that this has been done requires testing, inspection and market control and I would suggest this work could be undertaken by the officers of the fisheries research board working in conjunction with the fisheries officers in the Atlantic coast areas.
In addition, some encouragement should be given our inshore fishermen to invest in a mechanical clam digger or shellfish harvester. These are used with great success along the coast of Maine, and the fisheries industrial development service working in co-operation with the fisheries research board perfected 90205-6-299
Supply-Fisheries
a shellfish harvester called the "Cyprina" which they found not only good for clam digging but also suitable for harvesting "bedding size" oysters. The plans for this type of machine are readily available, the market for the clams is here in Canada as well as in the United States, and I believe this type of fishery merits a second look not only by our inshore fishermen but also by government officials.
Just what are the possibilities? While Canada's clam production last year amounted to $781,324 we still imported from Japan canned clams and crabmeat, another shellfish that could be processed in Canada, to a value of $482,958. It is true our clam production has been hampered due to contamination in certain areas. However, these contaminated shellfish further point up the need to accelerate construction of municipal and industrial waste treatment works to alleviate the evident destruction and waste of Canada's marine resources. It is a somewhat sobering thought that in the event of an atomic war the ocean could well be the only source of uncontaminated food supplies. The ocean is mankind's largest remaining source of edible protein and it cannot continue to be considered as an unlimited disposal dump for atomic wastes and the products of civilization.
The same conditions that apply to oysters and clams apply to a somewhat lesser degree to our scallop beds. This industry has grown in the past six years in Nova Scotia from almost nothing to a landed value in excess of $2 million. Some 25 scallop draggers carrying crews of from 15 to 20 men each operate on the offshore banks at Georges and St. Pierre. This is a deepsea operation and when landed these scallops are all inspected by fisheries' officers prior to shipment.
However, not too many years ago the bay of Fundy produced considerable scallops and these were landed at Digby, Nova Scotia. In 1927, for example, total production in Canada amounted to 39,000 barrels, and 37,500 barrels came from Digby. Due to overfishing and improper conservation practices this fishery has declined in recent years, creating a considerable loss of revenue for our inshore or Digby scallop draggers.
When discussing shellfisheries we must not forget lobsters, which had landed value last year in the Atlantic provinces of $18,041,000. However, here again is a commodity that is still in great demand not only in Canada but also in the United States and European countries, with markets apparently unlimited.
The export value of Canada's lobster catch last year amounted to $20,149,974. While this is a significant amount, we are only scratching the surface. I believe greater emphasis should be placed upon increasing the amount

Supply-Fisheries
of lobsters along our shores by establishing artificial breeding ponds. While this method of increasing available supplies was tried some years ago, I think around 1913 and 1914, at Long Beach pond and Gabarus pond in Nova Scotia without promising results, I believe that with our present scientific knowledge we could establish with a greater degree of success artificial breeding ponds for lobsters so that our bays and inlets could be restocked along the coast of Nova Scotia.
At the present time we are spending large amounts of money on research and conservation methods on the high seas with regard to our groundfish industry. The A. T. Cameron, a 177-foot research ship is searching out new areas for our ground fishing fleet. While I am vitally interested in all aspects of our fisheries development, I would point out that any new fishing areas discovered by the Cameron will only be useful in the future when we have larger ships than those presently in existence.
Our efforts to conserve the small fish by establishing net mesh regulations are also questionable as there is a growing feeling among Canadian fishermen that these regulations are not being followed by fishermen of other nations.
In support of that statement I would quote a list of prices taken from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald last week. These prices are for codfish in Boston. They quote large cod at 5 cents per pound, medium cod at 5.75 cents per pound, and cod scrod-that is, 2J pounds and under-at 5.95 cents per pound. Here the emphasis is placed on the small fish.
In view of our inability to enforce conservation measures beyond the three-mile limit of our coasts I would urge upon the government that we give more thought to developing our shellfish industries and those ground fisheries that come within the jurisdiction of the Canadian government.
I note, for example, the amount of the contribution this year toward fisheries research is only $25,000, as in the previous year, while the amount for the construction of departmental vessels has been increased from $200,000 to $980,000. For the reasons I have mentioned I believe more of this money should be diverted to fisheries research.
To encourage and provide an area for these developments I would suggest to the government that we give consideration to establishing base lines from cape St. Mary near Mateghan past Grand Manan island to the New Brunswick border and class the bay of Fundy area as a territorial sea in which fishing is restricted to ships of Canadian registry.

A similar base line should be drawn from Cape North in Cape Breton to Port Aux Basques, Newfoundland, and the gulf of St. Lawrence classed as a territorial sea, thereby providing an area for shellfish and certain groundfish conservation practices that would come under Canadian government control and provide an income for our inshore fishermen in the Cape Breton area as well as those in Prince Edward Island, the Gaspe coast, the Magdalen islands and part of the coast of Newfoundland.
I do not believe this action would receive any serious criticism internationally as Canada is bordered by three vast oceans, the Atlantic in the east, the Pacific in the west and the Arctic in the north, a total coast line of approximately 60,000 miles in which other nations have unlimited fishing rights. It would also have no effect on those countries which are presently fishing extensively on our east coast banks.
However, in the areas I have mentioned, where the base line would provide a small territorial sea, there are many fishermen and communities which depend principally for their livelihood on the fishing industry. We could carry out in these areas proper conservation practices and assist in the redevelopment of our shellfish industries, which could be of considerable economic importance not only to the Atlantic provinces but to all Canada.
With further reference to fish farming, I believe there is an increasing demand for more sport fishing particularly near urban areas, with the added possibility of developing a commercial product of value. I believe this matter was discussed at the fourteenth meeting of the Canadian committee on freshwater fisheries research, sponsored by the fisheries research board. I believe farm fish ponds and fisheries management should be further encouraged in Canada.
At the present time there are thousands of ponds, mostly in Quebec and Ontario, though we have some in the maritimes. In fact there is one in my riding near Lunenburg. The chief product of these fish farms is trout and the pressure on natural waters and the demand for more sport fishing is creating a situation in Canada favourable to the further development of ponds. There is also a growing commercial market for rainbow and brook trout, which at present are being imported from Japan and Denmark in increasing quantities. In fact, at the present time a 10-oz. package of rainbow trout packaged in Denmark is retailing in Ottawa for 57 cents.
I submit there is an opportunity in this industry for energetic Canadians, and I would urge the fisheries department to give every encouragement to this type of development.

Along the same lines I would urge that further consideration be given to the restocking of our rivers and lakes with salmon. In my riding we have fair salmon fishing on the Medway river in Queens county and the Lahave river in Lunenburg county but steps should be taken to build up the salmon runs not only in these rivers but in Martin river and Middle river and others in Lunenburg and Queens counties. This would further encourage tourists to visit Nova Scotia, and thereby assist in strengthening the economy of our province.
The recent loss of 17 fishermen by drowning when their long-liners sank because of high winds and heavy seas off the coast of Nova Scotia should cause some concern to the minister and officials of his department who have encouraged the construction through subsidies of this type of craft. These men were the very best and most aggressive or they would not have been where they were, and their loss leaves a void that will never be filled.
While long-liners were never intended to operate over 100 miles at sea on our offshore banks, I personally believe there is a structural weakness in these craft which would bear examination. The large wheelhouse placed amidships which covers the engine and fish hauler has been designed more as a shelter from the normal elements than as an integral part of the hull. When struck by a heavy sea this wheelhouse is quickly destroyed leaving the long-liner exposed to the elements and possible flooding when the next sea strikes. It is worthy of note that 65-foot draggers, which are completed decked over, and also ships of the schooner type between 75 and 100 feet in length successfully weathered this particular storm. As a matter of fact, the schooner type design which made the sailing ship Bluenose and the town of Lunenburg famous, has never been surpassed in seaworthiness. I would ask the minister and his officials to give urgent consideration to these facts and to the possibility of improving the long-liner design.
A complete study of the entire assistance program would in fact be most desirable. According to figures supplied by the economics service, Department of Fisheries, for the four year average, 1955 to 1958 inclusive, Nova Scotia draggers averaging 65 feet in length spent 179 days at sea per year. Here my remarks coincide to a considerable extent with those made last evening by the hon. member for Gloucester which would indicate we have our fishermen's interest very much at heart. During this period when the 65-foot draggers operated, actual fishing hours amounted to only 1,433, or less than 60 days out of a year's total of 365. This gives an indication 90205-6-299i
Supply-Fisheries
of the seasonal type of operation carried out by the six man crew on a 65-foot dragger and explains the reason for the marginal earnings shared by these fishermen.
It is evident these ships are not large enough to operate in the fisheries on a year round basis, and larger ships are required not only for the safety of men's lives but also to provide steadier employment at sea and ashore. This requires heavier capital investment, and in order to obtain this capital the fisherman must receive a better price for his fish. Of the species of fish landed it is interesting to note that cod, haddock and flounders comprise over 81 per cent of the total. During this period haddock landed averaged 3.5 cents per pound, codfish three cents per pound and flounders slightly better than 3.2 cents per pound. It should be pointed out that though fancy grades bring better prices than those previously mentioned, the scrod grades, that is to say, fish of two and a half pounds and under, lower the total average.
It has been suggested by many fishermen that the present price which has remained fairly constant for the past 15 years be raised by one cent per pound. This would make the difference between a marginal operation, and one economically sound and capable of supporting the fishermen and their families and supplying capital for larger ships. The next question is, of course, whether the market can stand this price increase. A recent survey in the Ottawa supermarkets on the three species mentioned showed frozen haddock in one pound packages retailing at 49 cents per pound, frozen cod at 37 cents per pound and frozen sole at 45 cents per pound. As it takes three pounds of fish to make one pound of fillets, an increase of one cent to the fishermen would increase these prices by three cents to the consumer. Even with this increase these seafoods which provide much needed vitamins and minerals to mankind would still be much lower in price than the trimmings from the slaughterhouse tables which are selling as hot dogs or all beef franks at 59 to 63 cents per pound.
An increase of one cent per pound on haddock, cod and sole over present prices would also go a long way toward providing further additional capital for use by our fishermen on the construction of new ships. While I realize much of our production is sold in the United States market, and we must compete with world exporters, I believe every effort should be made to provide at least this one cent per pound increase to our fishermen. To do this, we must encourage greater consumption of fish among Canadians generally. At present the average Canadian consumes 142 pounds of beef per year, 72 pounds of

Supply-Fisheries
poultry but only 13 pounds of fish or a little better than one pound per month. This despite the fact that fish protein has a high biological value in terms of body growth and repair. Fish protein is complete and balanced nutritionally. Fish protein is easily digested and readily available to the body. Nutritionally, fish are a gold mine of dietetically valuable minerals and of other inorganic compounds. It is now well recognized the serum cholesterol level in man can be lowered by reduction in fat intake, or by judicious substitution of one form of dietary fat for another.
In fish we have a uniquely valuable food; one that combines the biological value unique to the proteins of the animal kingdom, with the healthful soft fats unique to the plant kingdom, and which assist in the prevention of arteriosclerosis, a disease of the arteries of the heart. In addition to its health values, fish is available in a wide variety of flavours, textures and market forms. To the economy minded, fish fillets provide 100 per cent protein with no fat or bone to waste. It is readily available and easily prepared, and I trust it will find increased acceptance among our Canadian consumers thus providing a much needed boost to our east coast fishing communities, the secondary industries allied with fishing, and a strengthening of our entire Atlantic area economy.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Has the hon. member any idea of the price at which Norway is selling its herring to Japan?

No, I have not the slightest idea. I do not know the price of the kazanoko, but I do know that the coast of British Columbia is closer to Japan than is Norway, and that with a little research, and perhaps assistance in regard to trade markets, with the development of this new product, perhaps our fleet could have been operating instead of being out of work the major part of last year.
We have a similar difficulty in respect of our whaling fleet. My friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond can smile and laugh, but these are grave situations which should be drawn to the attention of the minister and his department.

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege; I was not smiling at the hon. member, but smiling at the fact that he has not bothered to produce the facts. If red China intended to purchase herring from Canada in the way it is now purchasing wheat, it would not hesitate to do so. The hon. member has not bothered to produce any factual information in this regard, and that is why I was smiling.

I suggest that the province of British Columbia, particularly its fishing industry, has been let down by this government. Mr. Chairman, I should now like to proceed to discuss a subject of importance to the peoples of Canada from the Pacific to the Atlantic, and I refer to conservation and the methods of killing in respect of whales and harp seals. I have been very interested in noting that only one hon. member from Newfoundland has made any mention at all of the sealing industry. Mention was made of the fact that a Russian icebreaker was at the icefields and that perhaps Canada might do something of a similar nature.
I want to speak on this issue from a different angle. Knowing that these estimates were coming up, I spent a most interesting two or three days a short time ago in reading the various issues in the past year of that most remarkable magazine, the Canadian Audubon, and the writings of that world authority, Dr. Harry R. Lillie. He had a most interesting article in the Daily Telegraph of Great Britain on March 19, 1960. It was
He subscribes to the hon. gentleman's political theories.
I did not catch that.
I interjected that the gentleman to whom the hon. member referred subscribes to his political theories.
To mine?
Yes.

I have read it very carefully. I say that the author lives in St. John's Newfoundland, and I am certain that the hon. member who interjected will admit that his long interest and knowledge of this very matter, tied in with the report of Dr. Lillie, should commend the article to the committee. What does the article say? It is something that in which everyone should be interested. May I just make a brief reference to it because it has to do not only with the methods of killing but also with conservation. The article reads in part:
The seal hunt is an annual adventure in the icefields to the north of Newfoundland. Full of hardship, danger and cruelty, it has been going on yearly for a century and a half, but is now near its final act, as the once great seal herds of the northwest Atlantic are relentlessly hounded to destruction by motor ships, aircraft and helicopters.
The article goes on:
Traditional toast drunk in St. John's to departing sealers is "Bloody decks, and many of them!" This is symbolic of the barbarity with which the seal hunt is conducted. Dr. Joseph Cunningham, the world-famous small boat sailor, who "went to the ice" in 1955,-
I believe this is the term used in Newfoundland. Dr. Cunningham went to the ice and found the seal hunt utterly degrading and cruel. The article goes on to point out what is happening to the seals off the coast of Newfoundland as they go north. He gives the figures of the Newfoundland kill. From 1831 to 1840 it was 470,000 yearly; from 1931 to 1939 it had fallen to 170,000 yearly; and now it is below this figure.
I have an interest in this particular matter for two reasons. I have a very keen interest in it because I take a great deal of pride in the fact that my late father introduced me to this question of humane killing many years ago. He himself never killed an animal or shot a bird; neither have I. That was the education he gave me; only kill because of necessity. But if because of economic necessity we have to kill, then let us do two things: one, remember conservation in the interests

of the economy; and, two, kill in the most humane way that science can provide.
I wanted to raise, first, this question of the fishing industry in British Columbia and the problems that we are facing there. It is my belief, as I said, regretfully, that there is not being carried out the research that is required to maintain the various segments of the fishing industry of British Columbia. Second, on the basis of the opinions expressed by authorities in British Columbia keenly interested in whale conservation and authorities in Newfoundland interested in seal conservation and not on the basis of personal knowledge, I submit that serious consideration should be given to this matter and we should be provided with information as to what the department is doing with regard to this matter which is of such great importance to British Columbia and Newfoundland. It is not enough to get an immediate return by killing now. Our great interest should be to profit from our resources in the best way we can, whether they be on land or in the sea, but at the same time to conserve them for those who come after us.
Irrespective of whether we are Conservatives, Liberals or C.C.F.'ers I think the great responsibility of a member of parliament as an adult Canadian citizen is to see that we hand on to those who come after us a heritage which is greater and fuller because it has passed through our hands. That is the principle I have tried to enunciate this afternoon.

Will the hon. member permit a question before he resumes his seat? I think it would be safe to say that we are ad idem on the question of conservation, but I was wondering whether the hon. member could explain why he thinks electric harpooning is more humane than the present method which I understand involves a detonation when the harpoon hits the whale.

I should like the hon. member to read the authorities I have been reading this past week, people from Newfoundland, the United Kingdom and Norway. According to all the information I have been able to gather, the exploding harpoon now used does not necessarily cause instant stunning because as a rule it hits the intestines and does not kill the nerve blocks. On the other hand, the electric harpoon immediately kills all the nerve blocks. According to all the reports I have read, it has been tested with excellent success. The request from the Audubon Society of Canada is that Canada interest itself in this matter and take leadership on the international commission-I have forgetten its name for the moment-in seeing that the most effective method of killing is used. Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on the estimates of the minister's department with particular emphasis on what I and many of us from the east consider to be a very perplexing and serious problem facing Canada's oldest industry. I refer particularly to the salt fish industry. As briefly as I can, I should like to tie in my remarks concerning the problems of the salt fish industry with the work of the fisheries research board. I realize that all too often people speaking on this subject tend to generalize and to oversimplify, and I hope that this afternoon I will not be too guilty of generalization, bearing in mind at all times that I do not have a really technical knowledge of this very complex subject.
Before doing so, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to what the minister had to say in relation to the community stage program. I too share the views of hon. members who have spoken in the debate, and state without reservation that in my opinion the community stage program should be enlarged and stepped up with all possible haste because in my view it is measures such as this that will assist in the salvation of the now dying salt fish industry.
The minister also referred in his remarks to the fact that last year was a good year for the Canadian salt fish industry, and the reason he stated it was a good year was the fact that European stocks were low. I think you have here the real weakness of the Canadian salt fish industry, the fact that our markets for this product depend upon the stocks or supplies of the European markets. It is a common fact that most of the European markets are supplied generally by their own subsidized fleets operating in most cases in Canadian waters.
To illustrate this, in 1959 world production of salt codfish was, I believe, approximately 350,000 tons. The Canadian share of that production was about 45,000 tons. I think it is generally recognized, as I said before, that the majority of this fish is caught and sometimes salted in the waters immediately oil Canada's east coast.
In relation to the problem of marketing and the sale of our salt codfish, one cannot escape reference to the system of marketing prevailing in the industry. The Newfoundland associated fish exporters limited, generally known as NAFEL, was abolished a few years ago by virtue of the fact that its exclusive licence as the marketing agency from the federal government had expired. This agency

Supply-Fisheries
was started by the previous administration of Newfoundland, that is, the government that existed prior to union, in order to correct a situation in the industry that was having serious repercussions around the world in the traditional markets for Newfoundland salt codfish. This situation came about by virtue of the fact that there was cutthroat competition and inconsistency in quality arising out of this competition, all to the detriment of the salt fish industry.
While there are many critics of this organization, there are many people who say it should have been enlarged to take in all of the east coast fishing industry including the Gaspe, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They say that it should have been set up as the marketing agency for all this area. I am not going to argue the merits or demerits of this cartel, because that is what it was, a private cartel with the blessing of the government, but I will say that just as a need exists in agriculture for a central marketing agency to dispose of Canadian agricultural products, more specifically wheat, in order to ensure stability in that industry and a stable return to the farmer, equally in my opinion the same arguments can be applied to the fishing industry.
I think that this fact is too often forgotten. By the same token, I believe consideration should be given to investigating the possibilities of the Department of Fisheries taking greater responsibility for the disposal of Canadian fisheries production, particularly of Canadian salt fish production.
There have been references to various types of salt fish, the heavy salted fish that is cured in Nova Scotia. However, little reference has been made to the light salted codfish, cured primarily by sun drying, for sale in the traditional markets that prefer this particular type of codfish. For one reason or another, this part of the industry has practically died. I think this is a place where the research board has a very important role to assume. It is a fact that in France, for example, a means has been devised for desalting heavy salted fish. The resultant product is even called "Newfoundland type" codfish. This is the type of fish they prefer.
Of course the problem, Mr. Chairman, concerns the method of drying. I feel that the fisheries research board is aware of this problem and is attempting to cure it. However, I do not think the industry is aware of the work of the research board. I hope I am not trespassing on the sensitivities of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, but I say that the experimental station at Valleyfield, Bon-avista, does not serve the purpose for which it was intended because it is too far away from the main plants that produce salt codfish.

After all, if it is not accessible to the industry it is logical to conclude it is not functioning as it was intended to function.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? May I ask the hon. gentleman if he has ever found the time to visit this research station before passing judgment upon it?

Unfortunately I have not, because Valleyfield is so isolated and so far away from the main centres of the island that I have been unable to go there. It is only a few years since the road was put through to Valleyfield. This is the reason why I have never been there. I grant that the establishment at Valleyfield is adequate in every way for the purpose for which it was intended. My contention is that it cannot serve any useful function unless it is close to the main processors of salt codfish. As everybody knows, they are located around the southern part of Newfoundland as for example in the constituency of my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo.
I am not going into the reasons for the establishment of this station at Valleyfield because I think hon. members can draw their own conclusions about that. I will say that this points up what, in my mind, is the weakness in the research aspect of the Department of Fisheries; the fisheries research board. I feel that if the plant at Valleyfield, or one similar to the one at Valleyfield, were located in a more practical location great benefit could be derived from it.
Referring generally to the question of the fisheries research board, I may say in my opinion this board has lost sight of its main purpose, namely to do the type of research, scientific and technological, that could be practically applied to the fishing industry. I do not believe this is being done. I should like to quote from a speech delivered by a member of this board in Halifax, I believe, not long ago. He said:
Be that as it may-here are the views of a member of the Canadian fishing industry who became a member of this board one year ago. In that period it has become apparent to me that the board lived and worked in a world apart from industry.
I believe that this is a very serious statement, and one that deserves the closest study. I feel it is essential that money be spent on scientific research but that the results of this research be directed toward the practical, everyday use in the fishing industry. I do not believe that it is enough for the scientists to examine rare species of fish. This may be a scientific end, in itself, but I say that unless the work of the fisheries research board can be translated practically to the industry, then it is not justified.

There is no justification, then, for the public money that is spent in support of this board. I believe there is room for research and more research, but let us put basic things first. I believe that the results of this research must be more practically applied in order to achieve its purpose.
I feel, for instance, that there should be closer liaison between the industry and the fisheries research board. I do not think it is enough to publish scientific papers because after all these have to be translated into lay terms that the fishermen can understand and that the industry can understand. When the minister replies, I should like him to deal with some of these points because I feel they are very important and basic to the future of the fishing industry.
In conclusion, I would sum up by saying it is my firm belief that, first, there should be a serious reappraisal of the policy of the Department of Fisheries with regard to the salt fish industry; second, I believe the Department of Fisheries should assume a greater role in the marketing of our fisheries production; third, I think the fisheries research board should re-examine just exactly what its function is and try to translate that function into practical terms for the day to day use of our fishermen.

Mr. Chairman, as far as the province of Newfoundland is concerned, we are today discussing the estimates of one of the most important departments of government. Newfoundland is an ideal base for fishing, not only for the Newfoundland fishermen but also for the British, French, Portuguese, Russians, Spaniards and others who come to the island every year with their fleets of ships.
These foreign fishermen, with their advanced methods and superior vessels, are fast outstripping the Newfoundland fishermen in methods of catching and curing fish. Consequently they can produce better fish at cheaper prices than Newfoundlanders.
At the present time there are approximately 22,000 persons engaged in the fishery ashore and afloat along our 6,000 miles of coastline. We have approximately 60 fish processing establishments and about 18 freezing plants. The industry ranks third in importance as far as the island's economy is concerned, and its products amount to $32 million yearly.
Newfoundland's main markets for salt fish were the British West Indies, Brazil, Greece, Italy, Jamaica, Portugal, Spain, Puerto Rico, Cuba and other areas in the Caribbean. All these markets are gradually disappearing. Many of these countries are now sending their own fishing fleets to fish on our Grand Banks off the coast of Newfoundland. This decline in our markets has taken place dur-90205-6-300
Supply-Fisheries
ing a period when the consumption of salt fish in these foreign markets, which at one time were our markets, is greater than ever before.
What are the reasons for this state of affairs? Some of the reasons for the change can be attributed to the tremendous assistance given to the fishing industries in these foreign countries by large subsidies and assistance given to these industries by the governments to those countries to build tremendous fleets of vessels to fish on our Grand Banks.
Another very important factor is the increasing capital expenditure for stores, boats, equipment, fishing gear, etc., which have to be made by the Newfoundland fishermen. Their costs of production are too high. Newfoundland requires substantial assistance from the government if we are to hold our place in the salt fish industry by regaining some of our lost markets and getting new markets in the foreign trade. Further, Newfoundland's switch to heavy salted fish has greatly reduced the demand for our fish in these foreign markets. We should therefore produce the kind of fish these markets require if we hope to hold them against foreign competition.
At the present time there are large stocks of heavy salted fish, much of which was caught by Newfoundlanders, on hand in the maritimes. A large quantity of this type of fish was sold to Cuba but owing to present conditions sales have fallen off and this is causing some panic selling by maritimers in the Jamaican market.
Now many of the fish dealers who for years opposed Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited-known locally as NAFEL -are asking for a form of centralized exporting. I am convinced that NAFEL should not have been cancelled by this government until it had a better system of marketing to replace it.
Much of the blame for the condition of our fishing industry today can be attributed to the lack of assistance, lack of initiative and lack of interest taken in the industry by our governments, as well as by the industry itself.
Our governments, both federal and provincial, have helped the industry in certain ways, such as a bounty on the building of vessels, rebate on salt, building fishing stages, etc. While these are good measures, this assistance is not enough if we are to be the great supplier of salted fish that we were in past years. If we are to regain these markets and re-establish ourselves in foreign markets the industry will need a tremendous push, the expenditure of large sums of money, much more equipment purchased and greater assistance given to the fishermen as an incentive to induce men to return to the fishing boats.

Supply-Fisheries
Newfoundland is finding it increasingly more difficult to retain her foreign markets and can have very little hope of gaining new markets without definite action being taken by the federal government to counterbalance and reduce to a minimum the difference between foreign fishermen and the fishermen of Newfoundland. Above all we need a fleet of our own vessels to carry our fish to foreign markets so that we can make all the money possible out of our own product, and to make sure that all the returns go to Canadians to be put into circulation in Canada.
I was very pleased to hear the statement made this morning by the Minister of Transport regarding assistance to the builders and operators of Canadian vessels. I hope it meets with every success, especially in our fishing industry.
In my opinion the salt fish industry still remains the main productive resource of our island home and should play a major role in the raising and maintaining of our economy at a high level. If we get the action, incentive and assistance required from all concerned, then the salt fish industry will have a bright future and will contribute to the growth of our island.
The salt fish industry still means very much to Newfoundland and to Newfoundland's economy and it will continue to play a vital part in our way of life. But its future will depend upon the action, interest and assistance of our governments, both federal and provincial, and a new outlook by the industry. The governments and the industry should act now, without delay, because time is short.
I am sure that all concerned were glad to learn that the government has earmarked $150,000 to continue assistance to the fisheries of British Columbia. The fishermen, I understand, will be paid 12 cents a pound for dogfish liver delivered to oil plants and collecting stations. I believe this grant was forgotten by the hon. members from Vancouver.
No mention was made of assistance to our east coast fishermen in a similar manner, but the dogfish is a continual source of trouble to the fishermen on the east coast, as it is to the British Columbia fishermen. For this reason I suggest that the same benefit should be extended to east coast fishermen.
The 12 mile fishing limit for fishing rights has been in the limelight again recently. To we Canadians, to the Atlantic provinces and especially to those in the province of Newfoundland, this 12 mile limit means very much. It means the difference between a sagging economy and a bolstered economy for our province. It means the difference between a small share of the wealth, and practically the wealth itself that abounds in these waters
around our shores within that 12 mile fishing limit. This is wealth which rightly and justly belongs to the people of Canada, the people of the Atlantic provinces, and in particular the people of Newfoundland, who have depended upon it for their livelihood for hundreds of years.
What is happening today, and what is taking place within that 12 mile limit? Fishermen from foreign countries, from Norway, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Sweden and other lands with their up to date ships equipped with the latest mechanical equipment are fishing our waters inside that 12 mile limit, taking the wealth out of our waters, taking from our fishermen, from our people, their means of livelihood, destroying our fishing industry and leaving the crumbs for our own fishermen with their small and limited ships which do not have the advantage of mechanical devices or modern methods.
What have we done about this? What has the government of Canada done about it? What does it intend to do to protect the God-given rights of our Canadian fishermen? Are we as Canadians, is the government of Canada, going to stand idly by and see our wealth being taken from us, our fishermen being deprived of their livelihood, our fishing grounds being used by foreign countries and our own fishermen struggling for a living against the tremendous competition provided by the foreign countries, while doing little or nothing about it?
It is up to any government of Canada, Liberal or Progressive Conservative, to see that our fishermen are given at least the same rights as those enjoyed by foreign trawlers. We were interested and glad to hear the Minister of Fisheries say on May 2 as recorded in Hansard at page 4254:
I want to assure the house that no avenue will be left unexplored, no stone unturned, in order to secure action which will result in greater benefits for Canadian fishermen in the waters adjacent to our own coasts.
Mr. Chairman, this is a matter of our own rights as opposed to foreign trawlers which very often violate those rights, rebuff our courtesy and disregard the need for conservation.
The national Liberal rally held in Ottawa last January recommended to the national council of the national Liberal federation as follows, and I quote from page 10 of the report of the rally:
We need a program for the stimulation of the fishing industry by increased assistance in the procurement of modern vesels and gear and by research in processing and marketing and in the promotion of expanded export markets. The 12 mile offshore fishing limit for foreign vessels should be established.

Recently two Nova Scotia fishing captains were summoned to appear in magistrate's court in St. John's, Newfoundland by the federal Department of Fisheries charged with operating within the three mile limit in Newfoundland waters. Yet foreign trawlers can come to our shores and legally fish to the three mile limit. This does not add up, and was never understood by the average Canadian citizen. We are glad to see that this situation has now changed and Canadian draggers can now fish to the three mile limit. I consider it is high time that this government gave further heed to the territorial rights of Canada and to the rights of her fishermen and took whatever action is necessary to see that Canadians have the assurance that their treasured possessions will be safeguarded through the exclusive right to fish within the 12 mile fishing zone. As I have already made clear by the quotation I gave, the Liberal party recognizes the need for a 12 mile limit to be enforced.
At the present time the seal fishing industry in Newfoundland is almost a thing of the past, and as a result of the returns from the hunt this spring, I doubt if any Canadian ships will take part in next year's seal hunt.
At one time, more than 400 vessels manned by some 14,000 Newfoundland sealers operated in Newfoundland and brought to port as many as 680,000 pelts in one season. This meant an annual expenditure of several hundred thousand dollars each year, and created much employment all the year round. Last year's catch had a value of less than $25,000.
This spring there were four vessels from Newfoundland and one from Halifax, manned by approximately 300 men seal hunting off the northeast coast of Newfoundland. The hunt was practically a failure, due primarily to ice conditions, and I would suggest that the minister give consideration to subsidizing the ship owners and the sealers.
Several requests for assistance were made by myself, by the owners, and by the captains of the ships who took part in the seal hunt this year to the minister responsible for the Department of Transport.
In view of what happened last year and this year, is the hon. member in favour of an international agreement on conservation?

Most definitely. In spite of what I have said about the failure of the hunt as far as the Canadian seal hunters were concerned, the Norwegians have been sealing off our coast for more than 30 years and seem to make a profitable venture out of it. This year about 15 Norwegian ships operated off the northeast coast of Newfoundland. This 90205-6-3004

spring, much to their surprise and regret, Newfoundland sealers found that in addition to the Norwegians they had another competitor in the seal hunt, a 7,000 ton Soviet icebreaker capable of cutting quickly through the massive ice floes which the Canadian vessels were unable to penetrate. The Russian ship was equipped with two helicopters which were used to scout for seals and then to transport the sealers to and from the patches of seals. The presence of this ship has discouraged our seal hunters and it is feared that if Russia continues to participate in the annual seal hunt off Newfoundland in ships similar to the one in operation this year, the Canadian sealing industry will become extinct.
The Department of Fisheries is well aware of the diminution of our seal fishery and the time has come-indeed, it is long past- for the department to take active steps to secure international agreement so that this industry may be preserved by putting a closed season on certain seals and limiting the number of seals to be taken each year. The season for seal hunting opens on March 5 in the gulf area and on March 10 off the northeast coast of Newfoundland. Until this year there was no official closing date. An agreement was made this year between Norway and Canada as a result of which, next year, I understand, the season will close on April 30.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief, but I could hardly allow to go unchallenged the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East regarding the attitude of this government toward the very important primary industry of fisheries. We all know that much has been accomplished, and that the qualities of the Minister of Fisheries will ensure that the problems of this very responsible group of fishermen in Canada will be brought forward and presented to his colleagues in the cabinet.
As an example of the progressiveness which has marked that department I should mention the fine new laboratory currently being erected at Halifax, and compliment the minister and his department for placing it there. The architecture of this new building is such that it will fit well into the complex of buildings in that particular section of the city of Halifax.
I should now like to mention a problem which is perhaps incapable of solution, although I hope it is not. The problem to which I refer results from a great deal of ice from the mouth of the St. Lawrence river drifting down to the coast of the maritimes causing considerable discomfort to the fishermen there. I am sure the minister is aware of this particular problem, as he announced just a day or two ago that the lobster fishing season in certain parts of the maritimes was postponed. Unfortunately, in the area in which I am most interested, from Clam bay along the southeastern coast of Nova Scotia to Canso, the reason has been opened on time. In some parts of that area this ice has presented little or no problem to the fishermen and they were able to place their traps and fish lobsters in the normal way. However, in other sections the ice has indeed presented a problem to the fishermen and has prevented some of them from fishing at all. In some cases the ice has destroyed the equipment of the fishermen. I have a report compiled by a number of my friends in that area regarding the losses of fishing gear. In the areas of Little Harbour, Ship Harbour, and the Tangier and Murphy cove areas, approximately 40 men have lost 25 per cent to 100 per cent of their lobster gear, and there have been additional losses in areas nearby. I do not have the complete statistics

as yet, but I will be making a visit there next week, and will be in a position then to bring details, as to the losses suffered there to the attention of the minister and his officials.
I realize that the fishermen do have an insurance fund which replaced the old fund of emergency hand-outs in cases of disaster, but some of the fishermen will perhaps be debarred from collecting under this fund because they were not insured. Since the community as a whole has been affected by these losses I hope the minister will be able to devise some formula of aid for these fishermen. Perhaps a partial solution could be found in the extension of the lobster fishing season which would alleviate the loss of profits to a certain extent, but would do nothing in the way of replacing the lost gear.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could be allowed to go a little afield of the subject for a moment or two, to relate an incident showing the qualities of the inhabitants of that area of Nova Scotia. They are very rugged individualists there. One week ago on Sunday, two fishermen accomplished a rather minor miracle in that they were able to provide a service to the United States which our own search and rescue team was unable to provide. A United States navy man became ill at the United States navigational aid installation at Hardwood island, which is about a mile from Sheet Harbour passage.
How far is that away from a Canadian city such as Yarmouth?

Sheet Harbour passage is in the riding of Halifax, which is in Canada.
On the day in question there was a wind blowing up to 45 miles an hour, and a very dense snowstorm prevailed. An urgent request for medical aid was received from the United States navigational aid installation at Hardwood island, and search and rescue were unable to answer it because of prevailing conditions. Two fishermen, David and Stanford Levy, of a somewhat picturesque place named Sober Harbour, with the help of sergeant Murray Cottell, of the R.C.M.P., conveyed Dr. Dennis Lahey to Hardwood island. When they reached the island they were marooned for six hours, unable to make the return trip. In order to make this trip they had to go two at a time secured by ropes in the dories. While the story amply shows the heroism and courage of these two fishermen and the mounted police officer, it had an unfortunate ending in that the individual who was ill had died before he could be brought to shore. This fact was unknown to the men when they made this perilous journey to Hardwood island.

I have related this story to indicate the quality and ruggedness of these two fishermen, who are of a type that can be found up and down the coast in that part of Nova Scotia.
In regard to the problem I mentioned at the outset, I hope the minister will be able to devise some formula to provide assistance to these fishermen.

Supply-Fisheries
economy, it must be expected that for the next 10 to 15 years those whose age and educational levels preclude them from being retrained and acquiring industrial skills will have no choice but to fall back on the fishing industry as a means of livelihood.
It is true that expansion of the fresh fish industry in Newfoundland has filled the gap left by the disappearance of the old banking fleet of sailing ships. Those plants have given a new lease of life to communities like Grand Bank, Fortune, Burin, Burgeo and Harbour Breton, which otherwise would have become ghost towns. Where these plants have been established the people have enjoyed relative prosperity but I should like to emphasize the word "relative" because the prosperity is relative only in comparison with communities which do not have fish plants. It is not relative in comparison with other industries either in Newfoundland or in other parts of Canada.
In my own province the best that can be said for the fishing industry is that it is holding its own. In many cases it is not doing that. The inshore fishery has not improved much in the past 12 years. It is true that the fisherman's lot has been improved to some extent but this improvement has come about mainly through the enjoyment of social security benefits which became available when Newfoundland became a part of Canada. The improvement has not resulted to any significant degree from increased earnings from the fishery.
This is not to say that nothing has been done. On the contrary, a great deal has been done both provincially and federally. The minister mentioned last night the improvement in the bait service and the provision of portable bait holding units and community stages. My colleague, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, referred to the small loans for fishermen and the hon. member for Gloucester mentioned the subsidies for fishing vessels. To these I think we can add the salt rebate, fishermen's insurance and other forms of federal assistance. On the provincial level we can mention bounties, loans to fishermen, loans to fish companies for plants and draggers and for modernization of equipment. In spite of all this assistance, which on the provincial level has been considerable in my province and possibly greater proportionately than that provided by any other province, the desired results have not been obtained. In my opinion the results that have been obtained have not been commensurate with the assistance given.
We may very well ask ourselves two questions. In view of this assistance, why is it that the fishermen have not benefited to
IMr. Carter.]
any appreciable extent? Second, what additional forms of assistance are required and how much if we are to put the fishing industry on a proper economic basis? These are two very important questions which can only be answered on the basis of facts. The facts can only be obtained by a special factfinding body set up for the purpose and armed with the necessary authority to get the information required. Since the fishing industry overlaps provincial boundaries, a body of this kind should, of course, be set up by the federal government.
As to the first question, why have we not obtained the results we anticipated from this assistance, though I am not in a position to quote facts I have been a close observer of the fishing industry in my own province and particularly in my own riding for the past 12 years. As a result of my observations I have formed some ideas and conclusions which, for what they are worth, I should like to put before the committee today.
In my opinion one of the main reasons why we have not achieved the desired results from all this assistance is the lack of an over-all, integrated program. I am not mentioning this by way of criticism directed at the minister or the government. I am stating a fact which I think has prevailed over a number of years. What we have done for the fisherman through all these various forms of assistance that I have mentioned seems to have been done on an ad hoc basis. These measures have not been the expression of an over-all policy.
The minister himself mentioned one or two good examples of that last night. He referred to the community stages. We have heard pleas today for the community stage program to be continued. Yet the minister told us last night that the program was one of 20 stages and as the 20 stages are completed that is the end of it. To what were these 20 stages related? I cannot see that this particular program of community stages has any part in any over-all program. It is something that grew up like Topsy. It fitted in as a type of winter works program. It was limited to 20 and now it is being cut off.
If the community stage program is a good thing and has a part to play in the development of our fishing industry, why should we stop it? Certainly it is one of the most important things that we need, and the very fact that it is being cut off proves my point that it is not related to any particular over-all program. Community stages are important for two reasons. They not only lower the cost of production but improve the quality of the fish. Instead of the fish being handled in many little buildings around a harbour it is brought to one place where it can be washed clean and sanitary conditions can be maintained. They

also provide the fisherman with an alternative in disposing of his fish because where there is a community stage the fisherman has a choice of selling his fish fresh or salting it. If there is no community stage he is at the mercy of whoever wants to buy his fish because he has to dispose of it at the only outlet available. The community stage program is a vital part of our fishery development program and I join with others in urging the minister to have it continued.
Another example one can cite is the salt rebate. This is a program whereby the fisherman gets a rebate of 50 per cent of what he spends on salt. Obviously the more salt he uses the more money he is going to collect by way of rebate. This encourages fishermen to produce heavy salted fish but in these times the market for heavy salted fish is poor while the market for light salted fish is good. We cannot supply the demand in Europe for Spanish cured and Italian cured fish and yet we have no program to encourage people to produce that kind of fish. On the other hand, we are encouraging them to produce a kind of fish which the market cannot absorb at the present time.
I think another reason why this program has failed is that the various provinces have had their programs and the federal government has had a separate program and if any effort has been made to integrate them it certainly has not been very successful. A good example of that is the portable bait holding units. As the minister told us last night, we have provided these at the rate of eight or ten a year. In Newfoundland alone we need at least 50. I think we could take care of most of our needs with 50 or possibly up to 75 but no more than that. Why should we have to dole these out at the rate of eight or nine a year and spread the small cost over a period of eight or ten years? They only cost about $5,000 or $6,000 per unit and if we had a program of 50 units for one year the cost would not be exorbitant and such a program would do much to establish our fishing industry on a sound basis.
Another reason, in my opinion, is that we have departmentalized our fishing industry within the boundaries of the various provinces. By doing this we have conformed to a clash of interests within the industry as between one province and another. The hon. member for Trinity-Conception cited the case of NAFEL, as did the hon. member for St. John's East. NAFEL, the Newfoundland association of fish exporters limited, came into being to deal with a situation under which we had to sell our fish to a central buying agency. Individual sellers were at a disadvantage in having to sell to that kind of agency. There were some undesirable features
Supply-Fisheries
in NAFEL, I readily admit, and I hold no brief at all for that organization. I do not think it was as aggressive as it might have been, but it certainly filled a need and the undesirable features could have been changed. It did not suit our friends on the mainland at that particular time, and they were out for NAFEL's scalp.
Eventually, the exclusive right of NAFEL was removed. Now we have the reverse situation because of that and because of the developments that have taken place in Cuba, whereby we are at a disadvantage again in marketing our fish to a centralized buying agency. The very people who wanted to kill NAFEL have now realized the benefit of it and would like to have it back. The point is not whether or not we have NAFEL back. The point is that we should have some organization to market our fish in a situation where we have to deal with centralized buying agencies.
In spite of all the assistance we have given to the fishing industry it has been so ineffective that foreign draggers can come all the way from Europe and fish on our very doorstep, producing fish more cheaply than we can and underselling us in the markets of the world. This morning the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador listed the problems of the fishing industry under three headings, production, processing and marketing. I would add two more headings to those, conservation and research. While it is convenient to separate our problems under various headings, this tends toward oversimplification because all these problems are interrelated and overlap each other. For example, the problems of production overlap the problems of conservation. The problems of processing overlap the problems of marketing.
My time is running out and I shall have to limit my remarks primarily to the problems of production. The fishing industry in my province is hampered by production costs. One of the. most important factors in that cost of production is the cost of living. Also the cost of our Canadian ships, the cost of their construction, maintenance and operation, is much higher than similar costs for the same kind of ships and equipment from foreign countries. The Canada Shipping Act regulations impose standards from which foreign draggers are exempt, and these add to the cost of operation of Canadian companies.
If we are going to assist the fishing industry by means of a bounty or subsidy, the size of the subsidy should be related to this differential between the cost of construction, operation and maintenance of vessels in Canada and the cost to our foreign competitors.

Company Directors
In addition, there is the cost of nets, twine, gear, processing machinery and fuel for the operation of motors. In this connection, the tariffs imposed on these items greatly increase our costs of production. I want to support the recommendations which the fisheries council made to the Minister of Finance to remove these burdens. We have done this for other industries. We have done it for the farm industry and, in some cases, for the logging industry. However, for some unaccountable reason we are reluctant to give the fishing industry the same kind of treatment we have given to other industries.
I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I have a few more items to mention. However, I feel this is a very good time for me to stop and perhaps I shall have another opportunity later.
