the second reading of Bill No. C-26, respecting company directors (directors' qualifications).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill as given in the explanatory note is to require that all companies created by the parliament of Canada be managed by a majority of directors who are either Canadians or Canadian residents. When this bill was first introduced two sessions ago, the requirements of the bill were a great deal stiffer in that they called for directors who were Canadians. Hon. members will see, therefore, that this bill is not now as strict or as limited in its provisions as the one which was first introduced. Undoubtedly, other changes will be required. What I propose to do today, Mr. Speaker, is to give the reasons why I think this bill is both timely and urgent and to point out two areas in which it might be modified. I would suggest also to the house that if it meets with the approval of the house it might well be read a second time and then referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.
I feel, for instance, it might be an advantage if the wording were changed to indicate that the majority of directors must be resident in Canada and that the majority of this majority must be outside directors; that is,
[Mr. Carter.)
directors who are not employees of the company. They could well have a financial interest in the company but would not directly be executives of the company concerned.
Another change which was suggested has to do with international, non-profit organizations such as governmental organizations. Hon. members will recall that recently the house approved a bill to incorporate the international brain research organization. Like other such international non-governmental organizations, the I.B.R.O. visualizes a governing board with directors from many countries.
A member of the press gallery has written an interesting doctoral dissertation entitled "Facilitation Problems of International Associations" in which he suggests Canada should do more to attract these organizations. I understand that currently the budgets of these organizations, as listed in the year book of international organizations, amounts to some $306 million. In addition, the total budgets of the intergovernmental organizations come to some $415 million. It will therefore be seen that the combined budgets of the international non-governmental organizations are actually bigger than those of the intergovernmental organizations.
At present Canada is host to very few of these organizations, though I might mention the international air transport association and, of course, the I.B.R.O. Naturally such organizations could not possibly be constituted with a majority of the board of directors being resident in Canada as these directors will be drawn from all over the world.
I should like to quote from an address given by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) at Dartmouth college on September 7, 1958. The Prime Minister said:
There is an intangible sense of disquiet in Canada over the political implications of large-scale and continuing external ownership and control of Canadian industries .. . Canadians do not wish to have their economic, any more than their political, affairs determined outside Canada.
I have heard many hon. members on the treasury benches make statements in speeches which are very similar to this and which I believe echo the concern of the Canadian people. In a booklet "Foreign Investment in Canada" by J. M. Smith, published by the Canadian Institute of International Affairs, on page 11 is found a table entitled "Non-resident and United States ownership and control in selected industries, 1954".
This information is taken from the Canadian-United States economic relations committee, page 104, which was a study prepared for the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. This table shows that the percentage of industry controlled outside of

this country in automobiles and parts is 95 per cent; in the rubber industry, 93 per cent; in electrical apparatus, 78 per cent; in chemicals, 75 per cent; in the petroleum industry, 70 per cent; in other mining, 57 per cent; pulp and paper, 56 per cent; smelting and refining of non-ferrous native ores, 55 per cent.
As hon. members know, the royal commission brought down its findings several years ago. This pamphlet goes on to state that the control and ownership, particularly in the petroleum industry, is undoubtedly much higher now than the figures given here.
In general, Mr. Speaker, one might say that we in Canada own and control the non-industrial spheres. We own the roads, hospitals, public buildings, houses and farms, but in our manufacturing industries and resource development industries we are at the best a very small minority participant.
This booklet refers to recommendations made by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects and I should like to refer to these. They can be found on page 393 of the final report, where the commission, in discussing foreign investment in Canada, had three recommendations to make. Before making these recommendations they set out that it is important that Canada should not discourage foreign capital by unfair, discriminatory action and that the free movement of interest and dividends to foreign investors should not be interfered with by currency restrictions. I quote from page 393:
We believe Canadians should have more tangible assurance than they now have that the people who are responsible for the management of such foreign-owned concerns will, whenever reasonably possible, make decisions that are in the best interests of Canada: that such concerns in effect become more "Canadian" in outlook. We do not suggest by this the development of a narrow nationalistic outlook; nor that the concerns in question should be restricted in their access to their parent companies and to all the benefits and advantages they obtain as a result. The following specific suggestions respecting desirable objectives for the operations of such foreign-owned concerns would not have these effects; we believe they would be of benefit to all concerned.
Then the commission makes the following recommendations:
(1)	wherever possible, such concerns should employ Canadians in senior management and technical positions, should retain Canadian engineering and other professional and service personnel, and should do their purchasing of supplies, materials and equipment in this country;
(2)	they should publish their financial statements and make full disclosure of the results of their Canadian operations;
(3)	they should include on their boards of directors a number of independent Canadians and they should sell an appreciable interest in their equity stock to Canadians.

I had one bill on the order paper in regard to financial statements. I am pleased to say that the government has taken it up in the form of a government bill which is a much better bill than the one I proposed. I sincerely hope this particular bill will commend itself to this government.

Referring particularly to the third recommendation of the royal commission, the final report goes on to say, as reported on page 394:
The third objective is that Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies-particularly the larger, well established ones-should sell some part of their equity stock to Canadians and include a number of independent Canadians on their boards of directors. A number of companies have adopted this policy and have said that it has worked out well and to their advantage. Certainly we see no reason why, if the Canadians selected as directors

were able and conscientious men, the adoption of such a policy would not work out to everyone's advantage. In addition to the fact that the public would have some assurance that broad Canadian interest would not be lost sight of in the everyday discussion and decision of company policies, the companies in question would be better informed of Canadian views and attitudes. Then the commission went on to say, as recorded on page 395:
The proposal that Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies should appoint independent Canadians to their boards of directors and sell stock to Canadians is, of course, not a new one. But fewer companies than one might have expected have done anything about it. speechtext:
I should like, in setting out this ground work, to refer to an address by Mr. R. M. Fowler, president of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, at the annual luncheon of the association in Montreal on January 27, 1961 in the course of which he discussed Canadian-United States relations. He had this to say as reported on the last page of his speech under the heading "The Basic Philosophy":
In the current debate about the extensive investment by Americans in Canadian industry, the problem is usually broken down into a number of separate issues. It is suggested that financial statements should be published, that Canadians should have a chance to buy shares, that more Canadians should be employed in senior positions and more research should be done in this country. No doubt all these steps have some value in themselves, but in my opinion all could be taken by a company and the problem would remain unsolved. A subsidiary can sell stock to Canadians, can have Canadian personnel throughout, can give generously to charity and so on, but if most of the decisions are made back in the home office by men whose interest in the Canadian operation is not greater than, and often less than, their interest in a dozen similar operations throughout the world then that subsidiary is not being a fully Canadian corporate

citizen. The first essential is de-centralized, autonomous Canadian management in the subsidiary.
I suggest that the views of a man with the international reputation of Mr. Fowler are well deserving of attention.
Again, in a speech to a seminar on Canada-United States relations at the university of British Columbia, Dr. John Davis, director of research for the British Columbia Electric Company, gave food for thought when he said that over half the profits of Canadian industry belong to non-residents, mostly Americans. That has nothing to do with the present bill, but Dr. Davis did go on to mention several complaints, one of which was the failure of United States subsidiary companies to appoint outside directors. He felt that Canadian industry could not operate and take its proper place in the economic life of this country unless there was a measure of control in the form of outside directors who could give to the parent company proper information and proper ideas as to how the operation of their companies could best be carried on in Canada.
I would refer also to the declaration of policy by the Canadian chamber of commerce for 1960 and 1961 as reported on page 39 where the following statement is made:
The Canadian chamber of commerce recognizes that a high rate of non-resident, long term, investment in Canada is essential to the continued development of our country's resource and manufacturing industries. However, it is concerned as to whether the non-resident owners are familiar, in all cases, with the principles underlying the Canadian point of view and thereby overlook or disregard legitimate Canadian interests.
Then follows the recommendation:
The Canadian chamber of commerce strongly suggests to the federal government, provincial chambers and non-resident owned businesses operating in Canada that it would be in the best interest of such companies to place or list their stock on the various Canadian stock exchanges, include independent Canadians on their boards of directors, employ Canadian citizens wherever possible, especially in managerial and technical positions; purchase their equipment, material and supplies locally when it is economical to do so, and publish separate financial statements on their Canadian operations.
A review by the Empire Trust Company of New York with regard to American capital and Canadian management, in queries to major United States corporations operating in this country found that those companies which had the most successful operation in general were the best citizens as far as the employment of Canadians, the appointment of Canadians on boards of directors, the publishing of financial statements and so on were concerned.
Perhaps the most recent publication is that put out by the Canadian-American committee and sponsored by the National Planning

Association of the United States and by the Private Planning Association of Canada. This booklet is entitled "Policies and Practices of United States subsidiaries in Canada." The authors of this booklet are Mr. John Linde-man and Professor Donald Armstrong. The former has had wide experience in the field of international economic affairs with the United States government and as a private economic consultant. He is the author of earlier studies on United States business performance abroad, published by the National Planning Association, and he is currently a partner in International Economic Consultants, Inc. in Washington, D.C. Professor Armstrong has had broad experience as an economic consultant in Canada and has recently been appointed director of the school of commerce at McGill University in Montreal.
At page 6 of this report the following statement appears:
In the preparation of the report the staff has benefited greatly from the advice and collaboration of a large number of Canadians and Americans in many different organizations.
Chapter 4 of this book entitled "Canadian-ization of Personnel" deals with the subject matter of this bill. I will not read all the details found in that chapter but will refer only to the conclusion. The paragraph contained in the conclusions section deals with the suggestion that at professional and technical levels Canadians are discriminated against. That paragraph reads as follows:
At the professional and technical levels Canadians already have an employment advantage over non-Canadians.
It shows that the record of subsidiaries in this regard is a very fine one. The paragraph includes the following statement:
A case might be made, however, for transferring to Canada some of the technical and professional tasks now being performed by the parent in the United States on behalf of the subsidiaries.
This statement refers, of course, to work in the field of research. It also is suggested in these conclusions that of the companies considered it was found that in many cases the nominally titled president was a resident of Canada while the actual executive direction in respect of all routine matters came from United States headquarters of the parent company, and from individuals who held no titles at all in the Canadian subsidiary.
It is also pointed out that the degree of Canadianism of a company is dependent upon the strength of the executive team. If there is a strong executive team at the head of the company the company will be more Canadian than a company with a weak executive team at the head. It points out that if
Company Directors
a parent company wants to make all of the decisions, almost invariably that company has a weak executive team.
In the conclusions at page 39 the following statement appears:
With respect to executive positions, there is a discernible preference for Canadians to fill the jobs available in Canada. The degree of Cana-dianization of such jobs is probably much greater than the meagre statistics on this point would indicate. However, titles and the nationality of the officer holder have little meaning in themselves. The important thing is the amount of authority that goes along with the office. On this point the interviews showed considerable variation among the companies, a variation which apparently reflects home office attitudes that cannot be changed simply by replacing U.S. executives in Canada with Canadians.
As was the case with companies with Canadian equity participation in ownership, it was found that decision-making authority tends to be greater in Canada among the subsidiaries with outside Canadian directors. This is not surprising, because most of the companies with Canadian equity participation in ownership also have outside Canadian directors, and most companies with outside Canadian directors also have Canadian equity participation. Whether outside Canadian directors will necessarily and automatically produce more autonomy for the Canadian subsidiaries is perhaps an open question. Much will depend on the strength of the men selected. But it is at least possible to assert that companies which give their Canadian subsidiaries a relatively high degree of autonomy are more likely than other companies to recognize the business and public relations value of a functioning board of directors with broad Canadian representation.
I think I have proved the case that subsidiaries of foreign companies would find it profitable to have directors who are residents of Canada and that these directors should, in the main, be outside directors who are not employees of the company. It seems to me, in view of the fantastic ownership of our industries, as I have pointed out and supported with tables which I have quoted, that this scale of industrial set up is not to be managed at the level of an annual meeting or luncheon held in New York or some other United States city. Absentee ownership may not interfere with plant functioning, or the efficiency of a plant, but certainly lends itself to a foreign outlook on the part of the companies concerned. The executive of a foreign company is not always a policy making executive, and it is in the field of policy making that it is most important that we set up a financing board and a policy making board which will interpret Canadian aspirations and Canadian conditions for the owners in whatever land they may reside.
It is quite true that the industry in many ways is putting its own house in order, but why should a good company do this when a poor company is allowed to get away without doing it. I suggest in this field it is in

Company Directors
our national interest to set minimum qualifications regarding the operation of companies in the same manner as we have set qualifications governing many other spheres of activity. We should also have qualifications governing the policy making sphere because I feel we are entitled in this country to have the industries which are growing here, profiting from the use of our natural resources and profiting from our domestic markets with almost life and death power over the economy of many communities, obliged to appoint as the policy making heads individuals who live in this country and understand the conditions under which the company will operate.
When I introduced this bill I pointed out several areas where this idea might well be modified. However, I suggest the fundamental principle is such that no hon. member in this house can quarrel with it. The fundamental principle is right and just, and I commend it to all hon. members for consideration.

assure you, sir, that I am not interested in a government or an opposition member fighting the next election. I do not very often agree in policy or politics with the hon. member for Vancouver South. Nevertheless, I believe that he should be thanked for his courage in proceeding with the bill before us because I believe it is in complete conformity with what we understood the government of Canada was going to do following the speech from the throne. It has not done it, but he has had the intestinal fortitude to follow through with a private member's bill. I was very sorry that the hon. member had to take half an hour to introduce the bill. I sincerely hope it will not be talked out because it was introduced by a backbencher on the government side of the house who is trying to put forward what we understood to be a principle of the Conservative party enunciated during the election campaign and in the speech from the throne itself.
This bill has only one major purpose in principle. Its purpose is to require that all companies created by the parliament of Canada after this legislation becomes law shall be managed by a majority of directors who are either Canadians or Canadian residents. That is an understandable thing. They must be either Canadians or Canadian residents. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have only one criticism of the bill as far as the explanatory note goes. I take exception to the words "Canadian residents". I wish the hon. member had said "Canadian citizens" because I know of many important companies in Canada-and a great many in British Columbia-the managers of which are Canadian residents but not Canadian citizens.

The hon. member spent a great deal of his time in being out of order, it seems to me, as was the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). I can hardly conceive that discussion of the business of the house and government business is in order in debating a private member's bill.
If the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wishes to find out such information it seems to me there is a proper place for such comment. The hon. member for Vancouver East made much of the number of members in the house a while ago. In view of the fact that he raised this issue I think I might say that he was the only member of his party in the house at the time. Perhaps he was using this method to point out the errors of some of his colleagues and perhaps I had better leave it at that.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member who introduced this bill. It seems to me he was far too modest in respect to the influence that the discussion of private members' bills on this and other subjects some years ago had on subsequent government policy and government bills. I think he made a most profound impression on the house previously, and inevitably on government policy itself.
The statement is made occasionally when discussions revolve around bills such as this and other measures that by bringing up matters such as this and by pointing to dominant United States ownership of Canadian industries somehow it adds up to anti-Americanism. I think the people who hold this view concerning such matters are exaggerating. The obvious answer-and the answer has been given by other people-is that this is by no means anti-American but by all means pro-Canadian. It seems to me that nothing but good can evolve from discussions that remind us individually and as a nation of the state of affairs in terms of foreign ownership and control, and if no other function is served than to caution us with respect to where these trends are leading us, such discussions perform a very useful function indeed. I was impressed by the statement that the hon. member read from the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, particularly the fact that it was noted that where firms had already in fact implemented policies in the pattern of their directorates which would qualify under this bill the results have been very beneficial indeed.
There is one aspect of the problem on which I wish the hon. member had perhaps spent a little more time, and I recall this criticism being raised when the bill was first discussed two years ago. I refer to the assertion, and to be fair I must say he did touch on one

Company Directors
aspect, that if such a bill became law it would create a class of professional directors or in a sense a group of front men qualifying according to the letter of the law but clearly avoiding the spirit of the law. Certainly this point deserves some attention. This aspect of the problem is perhaps superficial but I think it could and should be answered more clearly.
This bill and other bills and resolutions introduced by the sponsor of this measure focus attention on what has to be the utimate solution, namely, that Canadians are going to have to lose some of their investing conservatism and take a more aggressive interest in purchasing equity stock and participating through measures such as this and others. This is not an easy road and the investing habits of Canadians cannot be expected to change overnight. However, I feel that discussion and debate of matters such as this should be very much encouraged as they will ultimately benefit Canada. I should like to conclude by congratulating the hon. member and by wishing him well with this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) made some reference to the promise in the speech from the throne of a bill similar to that now introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome). The only reference I see in the speech from the throne reads as follows:
You will be invited to consider means by which to encourage a greater participation by Canadians in the ownership and control of industry and resources in Canada. You will be asked to approve legislation requiring the disclosure of information by business and labour organizations in Canada controlled from outside Canada.
Certainly it is the policy and the declared intention of the government to provide greater opportunities for the control of industry developed in Canada and companies operating in Canada. But the problem before us today and the motives which prompted the hon. member for Vancouver South in bringing this measure before us are found in the natural desire of Canadians to have the greatest possible control of our own assets as they are developed. The problem that arises is to what extent can we control the development of our assets by foreign investors without discouraging the foreign investment that is necessary for the development of the country.

subtopic: BOARDS OF FEDERAL COMPANIES TO HAVE MAJORITY OF CANADIANS
speechtext: Is it necessary?

subtopic: BOARDS OF FEDERAL COMPANIES TO HAVE MAJORITY OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
I think that is a matter of opinion. The hon. member speaks as if it is not. I think there is plenty of evidence to show that we have not got sufficient money of our own to develop the country as quickly as it should be developed. I know that the hon. member has the authority of no less a person than the governor of the Bank of Canada who said in a recent speech before the Canadian chamber of commerce:
... we are now at one more of the critical crossroads in our history, perhaps the most critical of all, when economic developments and preoccupation with economic doctrines of an earlier year are pushing us down the road that leads to loss of any effective power to be masters in our own household and ultimate absorption in and by another.
I think that expresses the fear of many Canadians at this stage in our development. On the other hand, I have in my hand an article written by Professor James V. Poapst, professor of finance at the university of Toronto, which appeared in the December, 1960, issue of the Canadian magazine known as The Executive. He attempts to answer Mr. MAY 12, 1961
Coyne's statement. The professor does not disagree with the desire and need of Canadians to take control gradually of their own resources and their development but in a very thought-provoking article he does warn us against haste in our nationalistic pride and desire to take over control lest we frighten away the foreign capital that is necessary in the meantime. He points out that discriminatory legislation seriously deters future growth when that growth would require large capital imports to finance it. Then, he goes on to say:
Let's not panic over foreign investment. If it does in fact create a problem, let's try a positive approach to its solution.
I think perhaps the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South is one for safeguarding this control. Whether or not it is timely, I feel, is a matter that has to be seriously considered. Professor Poapst said this:
In companies controlled by foreign investors, they decide whether Canadians are to be admitted as shareholders, participate in management, whether the company will undertake research in Canada, what products it will develop, where it will buy and sell, the prices it will charge, whether it will expand or contract. It is foreign control over decisions such as these that creates concern over "loss of autonomy", the greatest cause of concern over foreign investment. We are too sensitive about autonomy, inclined to think that any loss of it is bad. Yet complete autonomy requires economic self-sufficiency. Economic development based on specialization and trade involves the continued reduction of economic autonomy to acquire greater freedom from want. We should not try to avoid all possible reductions in autonomy but, rather, try to avoid any reductions that are not worth while. Canadians have benefited enormously from foreign investment. We lose sight of this when we become concerned with various aspects of autonomy.
Then, he goes on to say:
How significant is the fact that Canadian equity investors are excluded from many foreign owned companies? It is participation in total disbursements, not participation in distribution of profits alone, that is important. Obviously foreign companies pay wages to and buy goods and services from Canadians. Nor in an era in which about one half of net earnings are paid out in profits taxes can it be said that Canadians do not participate in the profits of foreign companies. Here taxation, which when applied to ourselves is described as punitive, is levied for our benefit. The number of individuals who would benefit directly from access to the shares of more foreign controlled companies is not large. While individuals are the major shareholders in Canada, share investment is narrowly concentrated among them. Institutional investment in shares is quite limited. Access to shares of foreign controlled companies could reduce the supply of equity funds for Canadian controlled companies. Finally, as it is, not all foreign controlled companies exclude Canadian shareholders.
Then, the professor goes on to say:
When a country commences to discriminate against foreign investors, these investors can be

expected to re-assess it as an outlet for further investment. This is not to argue that we must never discriminate against foreign capital.
Then, he says further:
There have been complaints that foreign companies do not give Canadians sufficient place in management. We lack comprehensive information on the distribution of management in these companies but in the study Canada-U.S. Economic Relations Gordon commission scholars, Irving Brecher and S. S. Reisman, reported on an examination of a sizable number of the larger ones. They found "overwhelming evidence of widespread participation by Canadians in the management of large foreign controlled companies". Also noted was an evolutionary process respecting the nationality of the managements. Foreigners who held senior positions initially tended to be replaced by Canadians as the latter became trained or otherwise acquired sufficient skill to do the job. Is nationality apt to override ability in the choice of management in companies where profits and not chauvinism guides decision-making?
I pointed out this aspect of it, not in opposition to the principle advocated by the hon. member for Vancouver South but because we know that during these days there is great evidence in all countries of a desire to control and benefit from their natural resources. I think perhaps the same situation prevails, to some extent, in the South American countries. Some of them have taken perhaps more stringent legislative steps to control their assets than we have. Perhaps that is why some of them have been slower in their development than we have. Yet, I feel it is timely for us, as Canadians, to examine the control that should be exercised over the development of assets of our country, and the legislative means that could give us that control without discouraging entirely the foreign capital that is desired.
